Chapter 1 · Tutorial 6

Pathology of Oral Infectious Disease

Bacteria, prions, fungi and viruses — what each does in the mouth, and how to tell them apart

The mouth carries more than seven hundred bacterial species, fungi and viruses, almost all of them harmlessly. This chapter is about the few that cause disease, and about the single question that sits behind nearly every one of them: has the organism changed, or has the host?

Know these cold

  • Actinomycosis = "lumpy jaw": Gram-positive branching anaerobe, sinuses, sulphur granules
  • Syphilis: chancre (1°) → mucous patches and snail-track ulcers (2°) → gumma of the palate (3°)
  • TB of the mouth: painless ulcer on the dorsum of the tongue; acid-fast, Ziehl–Neelsen
  • Pseudomembranous candidosis wipes off to a red base; chronic hyperplastic does not and may be dysplastic
  • HSV hides in the trigeminal ganglion: primary gingivostomatitis in childhood, labialis on reactivation
  • Oral hairy leukoplakia = EBV; bilateral lateral tongue; does not wipe off; marker of immunosuppression
  • Squamous papilloma = HPV 6/11, not premalignant; oropharyngeal cancer = HPV 16 (90%)

The oral microbiome and the language of infection

The oral microbiome contains more than 700 bacterial species, including ultra-small bacteria of the "Candidate Phyla Radiation" (CPR) group, together with fungi and viruses. These organisms colonise every surface in an ordered way — early colonisers attach to the acquired pellicle on the tooth, later colonisers attach to them — so the mouth is a stable community, not a sterile space that is occasionally invaded.

Two pairs of terms organise the whole lecture:

TermMeaningOral example
CommensalAn organism living on or in the host without causing harm, often with benefitCandida albicans, carried in a large proportion of healthy mouths; Actinomyces in plaque
Opportunistic infectionDisease caused by an organism that is normally harmless, made possible by a change in the host — immune suppression, altered saliva, broad-spectrum antibiotics, a dentureCandidosis after inhaled steroids; oral hairy leukoplakia in HIV
Acute infectionRapid onset, active replication, resolves or killsPrimary herpetic gingivostomatitis; herpangina
Latent infectionThe organism persists in a dormant state without causing disease and can reactivate laterHSV in the trigeminal ganglion; VZV; EBV; latent TB
Most oral infections in this chapter are opportunistic or reactivations. When you meet an oral infection clinically, the useful question is not only "what organism?" but "what changed in the host?"

The lecture groups oral microbial infections into four classes — bacterial (actinomycosis, syphilis, tuberculosis), prions, fungal (candidosis) and viral (herpes viruses, Coxsackie, mumps, HPV, HIV, hepatitis C).

Bacterial taxonomy

Classification provides a natural framework for organising diversity. Oral bacteria are classified largely by laboratory behaviour and morphology: Gram staining, catalase, haemolysis and coagulase tests; shape — cocci, bacilli or spirochaetes; oxygen requirement — aerobic, anaerobic or facultatively anaerobic; and growth pattern — clusters or pairs/chains for cocci, spore formation for bacilli.

Bacterial infections

Actinomycosis — "lumpy jaw"

Actinomyces are Gram-positive, branching, anaerobic or micro-aerophilic bacteria — A. israelii, A. naeslundii, A. viscosus and A. odontolyticus. They are commensals of the mouth and gastrointestinal tract, so the infection is endogenous: it follows entry into deeper tissue through an extraction socket, a fracture or a periodontal pocket.

SpreadBy direct extension through tissue planes — not via lymphatics — with a tendency to form sinuses and fistulae that discharge onto the skin of the face or neck
Pathognomonic finding"Sulphur granules" — yellow flecks in the pus that are colonies of actinomyces and filaments surrounded by neutrophils
Commonest presentationA chronic soft-tissue swelling that becomes a hard, board-like lesion with a lumpy surface, usually at the angle of the mandible — hence the nickname "lumpy jaw" disease
Tutorial 6 MCQ 1: "lumpy jaw disease" = b) actinomycosis. The hardness (induration) comes from dense fibrosis around chronic suppuration — the same chronic inflammation as in the midterm notes Ch 4.

Spirochaetes

Spirochaetes are spiral, motile organisms with a central protoplasmic cylinder. The oral treponemes include T. denticola, T. vincentii, T. socranskii and others. Three diseases to attach to them:

DiseaseOrganism
Acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis (ANUG)T. vincentii (with fusiform bacteria — the "fusospirochaetal" infection)
Periodontal diseaseT. denticola — a member of the "red complex" with P. gingivalis and T. forsythia
SyphilisTreponema pallidum

ANUG presents as painful, punched-out necrosis of the interdental papillae covered by a grey slough, with bleeding and marked halitosis. It is associated with stress, smoking, poor oral hygiene and immunosuppression — and in HIV it is one of the periodontal lesions that signal advanced disease.

Syphilis

Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum and runs through stages, each with its own oral picture. Learn it as a table — it is Tutorial 6's first short answer.

StageIntra-oral manifestations
PrimaryA chancre — a firm, painless ulcer at the site of inoculation (tongue, gingivae or lips), with regional lymphadenopathy
SecondaryMucous patches — raised lesions with a pseudomembrane surrounded by erythema — and/or "snail-track" ulcers of the oral mucosa, with regional lymphadenopathy. Highly infectious
LatentOften no clinical manifestations; a "mucocutaneous relapse" can produce non-specific white patches
TertiaryGumma — a crater-type ulcer that may destroy bone, typically the hard palate (and may perforate it). White patches (syphilitic leukoplakia) have been reported as potentially malignant
Tutorial 6 SAQ 1 — two oral manifestations of secondary syphilis: mucous patches and snail-track ulcers (plus lymphadenopathy). The gumma is tertiary; the chancre is primary — don't mix them.

Tuberculosis

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an acid- and alcohol-fast, slender, non-sporing bacillus. It does not take up the Gram stain because its cell wall contains long-chain fatty acids (mycolic acid); it is demonstrated with the Ziehl–Neelsen (or Kinyoun) stain, in which the bacilli hold the red carbol-fuchsin despite acid-alcohol decolourisation.

BurdenPreviously an invariably fatal disease. The lecture calls it the second most common infectious cause of death in adults worldwide and the leading killer of HIV-positive people. About 1 in 4 people in the world has latent TB, with a 5–15% lifetime risk of falling ill
SpreadInhalation of aerosol droplets
PathologyA chronic infection characterised by granulomas (with caseous necrosis); the primary site is usually the lung
Oral lesionsFewer than 1% of cases, thought to arise by implantation from coughed sputum. Variable, but usually a painless ulcer on the dorsum of the tongue
TreatmentCombination therapy for 6 months: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol (the four drugs for the first two months, then isoniazid and rifampicin)
Tutorial 6 MCQ 4: oral TB = c) painless ulcers on the dorsum of the tongue.

Updated figure. WHO's 2024 report states TB has probably returned to being the world's leading cause of death from a single infectious agent (after three years behind COVID-19). Quote the lecture's "second" in this unit's exam.

Granulomas here are the type IV hypersensitivity and macrophage–T-cell loop from the midterm notes (Ch 4 and Ch 6) — the macrophage cannot kill the waxy mycobacterium, so the response walls it off.

Prions — Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease

CJD belongs to a family of human and animal diseases known as the transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs), or prion diseases. A prion ("proteinaceous infectious particle") is derived from a protein that is a normal constituent of the nerve-cell membrane. The normal form is protease-sensitive; the disease-causing form is misfolded, resistant to proteases and to conventional sterilisation, and converts normal protein into more of itself. There is no nucleic acid. Spongiform describes the brain, which fills with holes until it resembles a sponge under the microscope.

  • Acquired CJD is transmitted by exposure to brain or nervous-system tissue, usually through certain medical procedures (contaminated neurosurgical instruments, dura mater and corneal grafts, cadaveric growth hormone).
  • Variant CJD, a subset, can be acquired by eating meat from cattle with bovine spongiform encephalopathy ("mad cow" disease).
Why a dentist cares: prions survive standard autoclaving, so infection control relies on single-use items where possible — and on taking a history (neurosurgery, dura grafts, growth hormone) before using instruments on high-risk tissue.

Candida and the mouth

Candidosis is the commonest oral fungal infection and the purest example of opportunism: Candida is a commensal in many healthy mouths, and disease means the host has changed. Species encountered in human infection include C. albicans (by far the commonest), C. tropicalis, C. glabrata, C. parapsilosis, C. stellatoidea, C. krusei and C. kefyr.

Testing for Candida

Culture (from a swab or an oral rinse "swirl"), DNA PCR, or a smear stained with PAS (periodic acid–Schiff), which colours fungal walls magenta. The catch, quoted on the slide: no test reliably discriminates the transition from harmless carriage (saprophytism) to disease (pathogenicity). A positive culture shows Candida is present — which it is in many healthy people. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by the lab.

Predisposition to candidal pathogenicity

Six categories (Farah 2010). Learn them as categories with one example each — Tutorial 6's second short answer:

CategoryExamples
Immune-modulating medicationsCorticosteroids (inhaled or systemic), immunosuppressants, cytotoxics; broad-spectrum antibiotics (suppress competing bacteria)
Blood dyscrasias and malignancyLeukaemia, neutropenia, chemotherapy
Dietary factorsHigh carbohydrate intake; iron, folate or B12 deficiency
Endocrine disordersPoorly controlled diabetes mellitus
Immunological disordersHIV infection, primary immunodeficiency, extremes of age
Salivary changesXerostomia (Sjögren, radiotherapy, anticholinergic and antipsychotic drugs)

Local factors complete the picture: dentures (especially worn overnight), smoking, and failure to rinse after a steroid inhaler.

Tutorial 6 SAQ 2: any two, e.g. inhaled corticosteroids and poorly controlled diabetes; or broad-spectrum antibiotics and HIV.

Classification

The names have changed twice. The lecture shows the progression; the current ("proposed") scheme drops the acute/chronic prefixes because they do not reliably describe behaviour:

EarlyRevised (1990)Proposed (current)
Acute pseudomembranousAcute pseudomembranousPseudomembranous
Acute atrophicAcute erythematousErythematous
Chronic hyperplasticChronic nodular / plaque-likeHyperplastic
Chronic atrophic (denture stomatitis)Chronic erythematous (denture-associated candidosis)Erythematous (denture-associated stomatitis)
—Chronic pseudomembranousPseudomembranous
Angular cheilitisCandida-associated cheilitisAngular cheilitis

So there are three primary oral forms — pseudomembranous ("thrush"), erythematous and chronic hyperplastic (once called candidal leukoplakia) — plus a set of "Candida-related conditions".

The three primary forms compared

Pseudomembranous (thrush)ErythematousChronic hyperplastic
AppearanceNon-adherent creamy-white patches or flecksLocalised erythema of the mucosaWhite, well-demarcated, slightly raised plaque; small translucent → large dense opaque
Wipe testEasily wiped off, leaving an erythematous, bleeding baseNothing to wipeCannot be removed
SymptomsRarely painfulMay or may not be painful (burning)Usually asymptomatic
Usual sitesSoft palate, oropharynx, tongue, cheek, gingivaeDorsal tongue and palate; buccal less oftenPost-commissural buccal mucosa, tongue, palate behind an upper denture
AssociationsImmunocompromise: extremes of age, poorly controlled diabetes, HIV/AIDS, corticosteroids, antipsychotics and anticholinergics, long-term broad-spectrum antibioticsChronic broad-spectrum antibiotics, chronic corticosteroids, HIVSmokers; over 35 years

The pseudomembrane is not the fungus alone: it is a mesh of fungal hyphae containing entangled desquamated epithelial cells, fibrin, keratin, necrotic tissue and bacteria — which is why it lifts off and why the surface beneath bleeds.

Tutorial 6 MCQ 3: pseudomembranous = d) white patches easily wiped off, leaving a red surface. "Cannot be wiped off" points instead to chronic hyperplastic candidosis or — in the HIV scenario — oral hairy leukoplakia.

Candida and dysplasia

Oral yeast carriage correlates with the presence and degree of oral epithelial dysplasia (McCullough 2002). The lecture leaves the causal direction open: did chronic candidal infection and its inflammation drive dysplastic change, or was the epithelium already dysplastic and the yeast colonised it afterwards? Either way, chronic hyperplastic candidosis is treated as potentially malignant and biopsied — see Ch 2's dysplasia features and Ch 4's carcinogens.

Chronic mucocutaneous candidosis

A heterogeneous group of syndromes sharing chronic non-invasive Candida infection of skin, nails and mucous membranes with associated autoimmune features (most commonly endocrinopathies). They are caused by genetic faults in the immune system, identified early in life, and oral lesions often precede skin and nail involvement.

Candida-related conditions

ConditionKey features
Denture-associated stomatitisErythema and oedema restricted to the denture-bearing area; related to poor oral and denture hygiene, nocturnal denture wearing and loose dentures. Usually asymptomatic
Palatal papillary hyperplasiaA papillary reactive inflammatory lesion of the hard palate that generally develops under a denture; common with mouth-breathing, a high palatal vault, ill-fitting dentures, night-time wear and poor denture hygiene
Angular cheilitisErythematous fissuring at one or both corners of the mouth, often with intra-oral candidal infection; also staphylococci and streptococci. Driven by a chronically moist environment — loss of occlusal vertical dimension or wrinkling, lip licking — and seen in iron-deficiency anaemia and vitamin B12 deficiency
Median rhomboid glossitisA symmetrical, erythematous, elliptical or rhomboid area of the posterior dorsal tongue just anterior to the circumvallate papillae, with atrophy of the filiform papillae. Associated with smoking and inhaled steroids (there may be an opposing "kissing" lesion on the palate). Biopsy yields Candida hyphae in over 85%
Linear gingival erythemaA non-plaque-induced gingivitis presenting as a distinct erythematous band 2–3 mm wide along the gingival margin; probably mixed fungal and bacterial infection; can occur without HIV but is markedly more prevalent in HIV
Note the caution on slide 39: conclusive evidence of a direct causal relationship between Candida and median rhomboid glossitis or papillary hyperplasia has not been found. Candida is present; whether it is the cause is unproven.

Treatment

First line: remove the predisposing factors. Antifungals come second, and only if that fails.

  1. Denture hygieneRemove the denture at night, clean it, and leave it out to dry. Soak acrylic dentures in 1% sodium hypochlorite once a week; soak chrome (cobalt-chrome) dentures in chlorhexidine once a week (hypochlorite corrodes metal).
  2. Oral hygieneAdequate tooth and tongue cleaning; chlorhexidine mouthwash.
  3. Steroid inhalersRinse the mouth (and use a spacer) after each use.
  4. Smoking cessation
  5. Antifungals in selected casesMiconazole 2% oral gel, 2.5 mL (half a teaspoon) four times daily after meals for 14–21 days; or amphotericin B 10 mg lozenge sucked four times daily for 14–21 days; or nystatin four times daily for 14–21 days.
Miconazole potentiates warfarin (it inhibits warfarin's metabolism, raising the INR — bleeding risk, even from the topical gel, which is swallowed) and interacts with some statins. Always check the medication list.

Dosing note: nystatin is dosed in units, not milligrams — the oral suspension is 100,000 units/mL, 1 mL four times daily. The slide's "10 mg" for nystatin appears to be carried over from the amphotericin line.

Candidaemia and invasive candidosis: Candida infection is usually localised and superficial, but in severely immunocompromised patients it can become systemic, with high mortality.

The herpes viruses

There are eight human herpes viruses. All are DNA viruses, and the property that unites them is latency — after primary infection they persist for life and can reactivate.

HHVNamePrimary diseaseReactivation / association
1Herpes simplex 1Primary herpetic gingivostomatitisHerpes labialis
2Herpes simplex 2Genital herpesRecurrent genital lesions
3Varicella zosterChickenpoxShingles (zoster)
4Epstein–BarrInfectious mononucleosisOral hairy leukoplakia; Burkitt and other lymphomas; nasopharyngeal carcinoma
5CytomegalovirusMononucleosis-like illnessDisease in immunosuppression
6, 7RoseolovirusesRoseola infantumShed in saliva
8Kaposi's sarcoma herpesvirusUsually silentKaposi's sarcoma

Apart from HSV-2 and HHV-8, over 90% of adults have circulating antibodies to each of these viruses — so most have had the primary infection, usually sub-clinical and transient, and usually in the first three years of life.

How a secondary (recurrent) HSV infection occurs

  1. Initial infectionVirus replicates in mucosal epithelial cells and is released as they rupture. Particles enter sensory nerve endings and travel up the axon; the viral DNA is incorporated into the nucleus of the nerve cell.
  2. LatencyViral DNA lies latent in the nucleus of the sensory neuron — for HSV-1, the trigeminal ganglion (the slide says "trigeminal nucleus"; the cell bodies are in the ganglion). No virus is produced and the immune system cannot see it.
  3. Secondary infectionA precipitating factor (stress, illness, sunlight, hormones) restarts replication; particles travel down the nerve to the nerve endings and infect mucosal or skin cells in the same dermatome.

HSV-1 — primary herpetic gingivostomatitis vs herpes labialis

Primary herpetic gingivostomatitisHerpes labialis
TypePrimary infection, usually in childhoodReactivation; 30–40% of the population at some time
Transmission / triggerDirect contact or saliva; incubation 5–10 daysSunlight; psychological or physiological stress; hormonal change
ProdromeMalaise, fever, headache, lymphadenopathyTingling or burning at the site
LesionsSmall vesicles that rupture into ulcers on all oral mucosa, including the gingivae; very painfulAt the mucocutaneous junction of the lip: prodrome → reddening → vesiculation → pustule → ulcer
Resolution7–10 days5–10 days
TreatmentSupportive — fluids and pain relief until it resolvesAciclovir 5% cream, 4-hourly, started in the prodrome
Active herpetic lesions are infectious. Defer elective dental treatment until crusted, and remember herpetic whitlow (finger infection) is an occupational risk without gloves.

Varicella zoster virus

Chickenpox (primary)Shingles (reactivation)
Cutaneous rash of vesicles and pustules, fever, malaise; highly contagious; pustules scab after 3–4 days. Oral: short-lived small white-opaque vesicles that rupture and ulcerate, usually on the palate and buccal mucosa. School-aged children; diagnosed clinically; symptomatic treatment. Establishes latency by the same mechanism as HSV-1.Unilateral vesicles and ulcers in a dermatomal distribution, preceded by a prodrome of burning, itching or prickling. Favours the trigeminal nerve — ophthalmic division most commonly (risk to the eye: keratitis and conjunctivitis). Middle to later life and immunodeficiency. Oral lesions stop sharply at the midline when V2 or V3 is involved. Post-herpetic neuralgia follows in a substantial proportion (lecture: >30%).

Ramsay Hunt syndrome is zoster of the facial nerve (VII) — the geniculate ganglion, with spread along the chorda tympani: vesicles and ulcers of the external ear, the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and the soft palate, with facial palsy.

Cytomegalovirus

Primary infection causes an infectious-mononucleosis-like syndrome; congenital infection causes cytomegalic inclusion disease with widespread calcification. Reactivation in immunosuppression produces pneumonia, colitis, encephalitis and chorioretinitis. Orally: atypical ulcers and an association with periodontal disease.

Epstein–Barr virus

Infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) is the primary infection in teenagers and young adults, transmitted in saliva ("the kissing disease"), with a long incubation (35+ days): pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, malaise, arthralgia and myalgia.

Oral hairy leukoplakia is an EBV-related epithelial proliferation producing white, corrugated ("hairy") plaques, bilateral, on the lateral borders of the tongue (also dorsum and floor of mouth), that cannot be wiped off. It signals immunosuppression: HIV disease, ciclosporin, corticosteroids, diabetes mellitus. It is benign, usually asymptomatic and not premalignant. EBV is also associated with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, Burkitt's lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Tutorial 6 scenario 3 — HIV-positive, bilateral white corrugated lateral-tongue lesions that cannot be wiped off: oral hairy leukoplakia; virus EBV; treatment not always necessary — it is benign and asymptomatic. It is a marker: it calls for assessment of the HIV disease and usually regresses as cART restores immunity.

HHV-6 and HHV-7 (roseoloviruses)

Seroprevalence approaches 100%. Primary infection is roseola infantum — mild pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy and fever, self-limiting. They replicate in the salivary glands and are shed in saliva.

HHV-8 — Kaposi's sarcoma herpesvirus

Kaposi's sarcoma is a malignant neoplasm of lymphatic endothelial cells. After primary infection the virus resides in endothelial cells; immunosuppression allows proliferation. It has been the most common neoplasm in HIV-positive individuals, and the commonest oral site is the palate (red-purple macules progressing to nodules), followed by the gingivae.

Other viruses — Coxsackie, measles, mumps

Coxsackievirus is a non-enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus (Picornaviridae, genus Enterovirus — with poliovirus and echovirus). Because it is not a herpes virus, it does not establish latency: no recurrences — the virus is eradicated and immunity follows.

HerpanginaHand, foot and mouth diseasePrimary herpetic gingivostomatitis
VirusCoxsackieCoxsackieHSV-1
Oral lesionsNumerous small vesicles (1–2 mm) mostly on the pillars of the fauces, uvula, tonsils and soft palate — the back of the mouthSmall vesicles on the oral mucosaVesicles and ulcers on all oral mucosa
GingivaeNot commonly affectedVariableAffected — a key discriminator
Elsewhere—Palms of the hands and soles of the feet — the extra-oral lesions distinguish it—
CourseFever and sore throat for ~2 days, then vesicles for 3–4 daysIncubation 2–6 days; preschool outbreaksIncubation 5–10 days; resolves 7–10 days
RecurrenceNoNoYes — as herpes labialis

Paramyxoviruses — measles and mumps

Measles (morbillivirus)Mumps (rubulavirus)
Incubation10–12 days; infectious from about 2 days before symptoms until 4 days after the rash appears14–21 days
IllnessProdrome of fever, malaise, coryza, conjunctivitis and cough → exanthematous rash beginning on the faceMalaise, anorexia, fever and sialadenitis
Oral signKoplik spots — red spots with blue-white specks on the buccal mucosa, appearing in the prodrome before the rashBilateral parotid swelling (occasionally submandibular, or unilateral); saliva remains normal despite ductal inflammation
PreventionMMR vaccine

Human papillomavirus

HPV is a group of DNA viruses with about 200 identified sub-types, classified by tissue tropism into dermatotropic (skin) and mucosotropic types. It is transmitted by direct contact with an infected lesion. Infection is very common — a female lifetime risk of 50–80% — and most people clear it; 10–15% of women fail to mount an adequate T-cell response and develop persistent infection, which is where the cancer risk lies. In cervical cancer, HPV 16 is found in 50–70% and HPV 18 in 7–20%.

Oral HPV infection (US adults 18–69, oral rinse PCR, 2011–14): any type in 11.5% of men and 3.2% of women; high-risk HPV 16 or 18 in 7.3% of men and 1.4% of women.

The benign oral HPV lesions

LesionHPV typesFeaturesTreatment
Squamous papilloma6 and 11 (most commonly)The commonest oral HPV lesion: finger-like projections giving a rough, cauliflower surface; white or pink depending on keratinisation; usually single; no symptoms and no known malignant potentialSurgical removal
Verruca vulgarisLecture: 1 and 57 (most texts: 2 and 4)The common skin wart (hands) that can appear in the mouth, often from finger-sucking or nail-biting; clinically and histologically like a squamous papillomaSurgical removal
Condyloma acuminatumLecture: 2, 6 and 11 (chiefly 6 and 11)Genital wart that can occur orally after sexual transmission (oral sex); multiple wartsSurgical removal
Multifocal epithelial hyperplasia (Heck's disease)13 and 32Children in crowded conditions; First Nations and Indigenous Australian communities. Multiple soft, flat or rounded nodules, mucosa-coloured, on buccal and labial mucosa; disappear when the mucosa is stretched; regress with ageRemoval only if required for appearance
Tutorial 6 scenario 2 — multiple white papillary projections, HPV 6: squamous papilloma; not premalignant; surgical excision including the base, and histology to confirm. (Multiple lesions in an adult should prompt you to consider condyloma and immune status.)

HPV and head and neck cancer

Proportion40–80% of oropharyngeal cancers are HPV-positive
SitesBase of tongue and tonsils — often presenting as an enlarged neck mass, which is why we palpate the lymph nodes
TypesHPV 16, 18, 31 and 33 — and 90% are HPV 16. The same types cause cervical cancer
Oral cavityLittle to no role — about 3.6% of oral cavity cancers. Oropharynx ≠ oral cavity
VaccineGardasil (9-valent) targets HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58
Tutorial 6 MCQ 5: c) HPV 16. The mechanism — E6 degrades p53, E7 inactivates pRb — is in Ch 3 (Viral carcinogenesis) and Ch 4.

HIV in the infection lecture

The pathogenesis and staging of HIV are in the midterm notes (Ch 8). Lecture 6 adds epidemiology, treatment and prevention:

Global (as presented, 2017–18)About 37.9 million living with HIV at the end of 2018; 1.7 million newly infected in 2017; the WHO African Region carries 25.7 million and almost two-thirds of new infections; 62% of adults and 54% of children were on lifelong ART. Deaths fell to 940,000 in 2017 — given on the slide as a 47% reduction since the 1996 peak
In UNAIDS reporting the late-1990s peak is the peak of new infections; AIDS-related deaths peaked in 2004 (UNAIDS 2019: new infections −40% since 1997, deaths −56% since 2004)
Australia (2017)27,545 people estimated HIV-positive; 2,899 unaware. Prevalence: gay and bisexual men 7.9%; people who inject drugs 0.7%; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people 0.11%; all adults 0.14%
TransmissionSexual intercourse; parenteral; vertical
CoursePrimary infection ("flu-like" acute seroconversion syndrome) → chronic carriage → opportunistic infections related to CD4+ lymphocyte dysfunction → AIDS

Treatment and prevention

Combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) draws on five classes: nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs, "nukes"); non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs, "non-nukes"); protease inhibitors; integrase inhibitors; and entry inhibitors — each blocking a different step of the viral life cycle.

StrategyWhat it is
PrEP — pre-exposure prophylaxisRegular HIV medication (tenofovir + emtricitabine) taken by HIV-negative people to prevent acquisition
PEP — post-exposure prophylaxisA 28-day course, which must be started within 72 hours of exposure (e.g. a needlestick)
U = UUndetectable equals untransmittable. The Opposites Attract study (343 serodiscordant gay couples in Australia, Bangkok and Rio de Janeiro) found no HIV transmission in 16,889 acts of condomless anal sex when the HIV-positive partner's virus was fully suppressed on treatment

Most common oral manifestations of HIV worldwide

  • Candidosis (with or without pharyngeal involvement) — pseudomembranous, erythematous, hyperplastic, angular cheilitis
  • Oral hairy leukoplakia
  • Recurrent aphthous-like ulceration
  • Oral Kaposi's sarcoma
  • Oral herpes viruses (simplex and zoster)
  • HPV (wart-like) lesions
  • Periodontal diseases — linear gingival erythema, necrotising ulcerative gingivitis, necrotising ulcerative periodontitis
Tutorial 6 MCQ 2: most commonly associated with HIV = a) oral hairy leukoplakia. Median rhomboid glossitis, pyostomatitis vegetans and amalgam tattoo are not HIV lesions.

Hepatitis C

CourseIncubation 6–12 weeks (WHO: 2 weeks to 6 months). Acute disease → chronic active hepatitis → cirrhosis → (hepatocellular carcinoma). Most infected people (lecture: 80%; WHO: about 70%) develop chronic infection
TransmissionBlood-borne. Virus is present in blood, saliva and semen
Needlestick riskAbout 3% (compare HIV 0.3%, HBV ~30%) — and there is no vaccine

Oral findings in HCV

  • Sjögren-like sialadenitis — in one study 50% of people with HCV had lymphocytic infiltration of the salivary glands, causing gland destruction and reduced output
  • Xerostomia — complained of by about 50%
  • Increased risk of salivary gland lymphoma
  • Association with oral lichen planus
  • A possible increased risk of oral squamous cell carcinoma; case reports of Behçet's disease and vesiculobullous conditions

Hepatitis C can be cured

Direct-acting antivirals are listed on the PBS (daclatasvir; sofosbuvir alone or combined with velpatasvir, ledipasvir, or velpatasvir and voxilaprevir; glecaprevir/pibrentasvir; elbasvir/grazoprevir). The lecture quotes cure rates of 40–80% depending on genotype.

Updated figure. WHO currently states that direct-acting antivirals cure more than 95% of people with hepatitis C; the 40–80% figure reflects older regimens. Either way, HCV is now a curable infection — unlike HBV and HIV.

Required reading: Cawson and Odell, Cawson's Essentials of Oral Pathology and Oral Medicine, 8th ed., Chapter 13; and 9th ed. (Odell 2017), Chapter 16, pp. 256–282.

Drill

Two white lesions: one on the soft palate that rubs off with gauze leaving a bleeding surface; one on the lateral tongue that will not rub off. Name the possibilities for each and how you would decide.

The one that wipes off is pseudomembranous candidosis — the pseudomembrane of hyphae, desquamated cells, fibrin and bacteria lifts away from an erythematous base. Confirm with a PAS-stained smear and look for the predisposing factor (steroid inhaler, antibiotics, diabetes, HIV). The one that does not wipe off could be chronic hyperplastic candidosis (post-commissural, smoker, over 35), oral hairy leukoplakia (bilateral, corrugated, immunosuppressed), frictional keratosis or leukoplakia. Because chronic hyperplastic candidosis is associated with dysplasia, a persistent non-removable white patch is biopsied.

A 6-year-old has fever and painful vesicles and ulcers. How do you separate primary herpetic gingivostomatitis, herpangina and hand, foot and mouth disease?

Look at where the lesions are. HSV affects all oral mucosa including the gingivae, which are swollen and red. Herpangina (Coxsackie) is confined to the back of the mouth — fauces, uvula, tonsils, soft palate — and spares the gingivae. Hand, foot and mouth disease has lesions on the palms and soles as well. Only HSV recurs, because only herpes viruses establish latency; Coxsackie is eradicated and leaves immunity.

Explain why herpes labialis recurs on the same part of the same lip.

During primary infection HSV-1 enters sensory nerve endings and travels up the axon to the trigeminal ganglion, where its DNA lies latent in the neuron's nucleus. A trigger (sunlight, stress, illness, hormones) restarts replication; the virus travels back down the same sensory fibres to the skin or mucosa they supply — the same patch of lip each time.

Why is "cultured Candida from the lesion" not enough to diagnose candidosis?

Because Candida is a commensal in many healthy mouths, and no single test distinguishes carriage from disease. The diagnosis is clinical — a typical lesion plus a predisposing factor — supported by a positive smear or culture, and confirmed by response when the predisposing factor is removed.

A neck lump in a 52-year-old non-smoker with a small lesion at the base of the tongue. What is the likely link, and why is the oral cavity different?

High-risk HPV — 90% HPV 16 — causing oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil or base of tongue, which often presents first as a nodal metastasis. HPV is implicated in 40–80% of oropharyngeal cancers but only about 3.6% of oral cavity cancers, where tobacco and alcohol remain dominant.

Tutorial 6 — answer key

MCQ 1 — "lumpy jaw disease"
b) Actinomycosis.
MCQ 2 — most commonly associated with HIV
a) Oral hairy leukoplakia.
MCQ 3 — hallmark of pseudomembranous candidosis
d) White patches that are easily wiped off, leaving a red surface.
MCQ 4 — oral lesions of tuberculosis
c) Painless ulcers on the dorsum of the tongue.
MCQ 5 — HPV most strongly associated with oropharyngeal cancer
c) HPV 16.
SAQ — two oral manifestations of secondary syphilis
Mucous patches (raised lesions with a pseudomembrane and an erythematous halo) and snail-track ulcers; regional lymphadenopathy accompanies them.
SAQ — two predisposing factors for oral candidosis
Any two from: corticosteroids (inhaled or systemic) and other immune-modulating drugs; broad-spectrum antibiotics; poorly controlled diabetes; HIV or other immunodeficiency; xerostomia; blood dyscrasias and malignancy; iron/B12 deficiency; dentures worn at night; smoking; extremes of age.
SAQ — two herpes viruses causing oral lesions
HSV-1 (primary herpetic gingivostomatitis, herpes labialis) and VZV (chickenpox, shingles); also EBV (oral hairy leukoplakia), CMV (atypical ulcers), HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma).
Scenario 1 — overnight denture wearer, erythematous palate
Diagnosis: denture-associated stomatitis (erythematous candidosis). Management: denture hygiene with weekly soak — 1% sodium hypochlorite for acrylic, chlorhexidine for chrome; oral hygiene and chlorhexidine rinse; review fit; antifungal (e.g. miconazole gel to the fitting surface) only if this fails — check for warfarin first. Advice: remove the denture at night, clean it, and leave it out to dry.
Scenario 2 — white papillary projections, HPV 6
Squamous papilloma; not premalignant; surgical excision including the base, with histological confirmation.
Scenario 3 — HIV, bilateral corrugated lateral-tongue lesions that do not wipe off
Oral hairy leukoplakia; Epstein–Barr virus; treatment not usually necessary — benign and asymptomatic, but a marker of immunosuppression that warrants review of HIV control (it tends to regress with effective cART).

Chapter 2 · Tutorial 7A

Neoplasia 1 — Nomenclature & Features

What makes a growth a neoplasm, what makes a neoplasm malignant, and how it harms the patient

Every adaptation in the midterm notes (Ch 2) regresses when its stimulus is removed. A neoplasm does not — it has become autonomous. This chapter fixes the vocabulary, the benign-versus-malignant criteria, and the effects a tumour has on the person carrying it.

Know these cold

  • Neoplasm = abnormal growth of cells that persists in the absence of the initiating stimulus
  • Invasion and metastasis are the only absolute discriminators of malignancy
  • Malignant cytology: frequent/atypical mitoses, anaplasia, pleomorphism, hyperchromatism, ↑ N:C ratio
  • -oma benign; carcinoma = epithelial; sarcoma = mesenchymal; adenoma/adenocarcinoma = glandular
  • Malignant despite -oma: lymphoma, melanoma, mesothelioma, seminoma
  • Anaplasia = lack of differentiation; a reliable indicator of malignancy
  • Dysplasia: drop-shaped rete ridges, superficial mitoses; benign harm = pressure, obstruction, hormone, transformation, anxiety

Tumour and neoplasm

Tumour has two meanings — an abnormal swelling, or a neoplasm — so it is loose: an abscess or a haematoma is a swelling too. A neoplasm is a lesion resulting from the autonomous or relatively autonomous abnormal growth of cells that persists in the absence of the initiating stimulus. The phrase that carries the definition is "persists in the absence of the initiating stimulus": hypertrophy, hyperplasia and metaplasia (midterm Ch 2) all regress when the stimulus is removed; a neoplasm does not. Every neoplasm is a tumour; not every tumour is a neoplasm.

Tutorial 7A MCQ 1: neoplasm = d) abnormal growth that persists in the absence of the initiating stimulus.

A neoplasm has two components: the parenchyma — the transformed, neoplastic cells, the tumour proper — and the stroma — host-derived supporting connective tissue, the route by which the tumour gets its blood supply (and later, its angiogenesis, Chapter 3).

Benign and malignant

Benign: microscopic and gross characteristics are relatively innocent, implying the lesion will remain localised and is amenable to local surgical removal. Malignant: the lesion can invade and destroy adjacent structures and spread to distant sites (metastasise) to cause death.

FeatureBenignMalignant
Growth rateSlowRelatively rapid
MitosesInfrequent, normalFrequent and atypical (tripolar, asymmetric)
Resemblance to normal tissue (differentiation)GoodVariable, often poor — anaplasia
Nuclear morphologyNear normalEnlarged, hyperchromatic, irregular outline, multiple/prominent nucleoli, pleomorphic (variable size and shape); high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio
BorderCircumscribed, often encapsulated (compressed surrounding tissue)Poorly defined, infiltrative
Growth on a surfaceOften exophytic — piles up outward; pedunculated or sessileOften endophytic — burrows in; ulcerated, indurated, rolled everted margin, fixed
Necrosis / haemorrhageRareCommon — outgrows supply; bleeds from ulcerated surfaces
InvasionNoYes — breaches basement membrane, infiltrates stroma, perineural and vascular spaces
MetastasisNoYes — lymphatic (carcinomas), haematogenous (sarcomas), transcoelomic

Invasion and metastasis are the only absolute discriminators. Everything else — growth rate, mitoses, nuclear appearance — is a tendency with exceptions. A slow-growing, well-differentiated lesion that invades is still malignant. Clinically, an ulcerated, indurated lesion with rolled margins worries you more than a pedunculated lump.

Tutorial 7A MCQ 3: malignant = b) frequent mitoses and anaplasia. MCQ 4: anaplasia = b) decreased differentiation.

Nomenclature

Names encode tissue of origin (root) and behaviour (suffix). Learn the root and the suffix separately and most names decode themselves — apart from four exceptions.

Tissue of originBenignMalignant
Squamous epitheliumSquamous papillomaSquamous cell carcinoma — by far the commonest oral malignancy
Glandular / ductal epitheliumAdenoma (cystadenoma if cystic)Adenocarcinoma — grows in a glandular pattern (thyroid, colon, salivary)
Transitional epitheliumTransitional cell papillomaTransitional (urothelial) carcinoma
Fibrous tissueFibromaFibrosarcoma
FatLipomaLiposarcoma
CartilageChondromaChondrosarcoma
BoneOsteomaOsteosarcoma
Smooth / skeletal muscleLeiomyoma / rhabdomyomaLeiomyosarcoma / rhabdomyosarcoma
Blood vesselsHaemangiomaAngiosarcoma (Kaposi's sarcoma)
MelanocytesNaevusMelanoma
Lymphoid / haemopoietic—Lymphoma, leukaemia, myeloma
OdontogenicAmeloblastoma (benign but locally aggressive), odontomaAmeloblastic carcinoma (rare)
TermMeaning
-omaBenign neoplasm (fibroma, chondroma, adenoma)
CarcinomaMalignant neoplasm of epithelial cells, regardless of tissue of origin
AdenocarcinomaMalignant neoplasm of glandular or ductal epithelium growing in a glandular pattern
SarcomaMalignant neoplasm of solid mesenchymal (connective) tissue
-blastomaEmbryonal tumour (retinoblastoma, neuroblastoma)
TeratomaGerm-cell tumour with derivatives of more than one germ layer
Hamartoma / choristomaDisorganised but mature native tissue / normal tissue in an abnormal site — not true neoplasms
-oma but malignant: lymphoma, melanoma, mesothelioma, seminoma (add leukaemia, hepatoma, glioma). "Malignant melanoma" is redundant; the benign counterpart is a naevus. Tutorial 7A MCQ 2: benign glandular = c) adenoma.

Differentiation, anaplasia and dysplasia

Differentiation is the extent to which a neoplasm resembles its parenchymal cells of origin, morphologically and functionally. Well-differentiated tumours keep the architecture and products of the parent tissue (keratin pearls in SCC, hormone secretion in an adenoma). Anaplasia is lack of differentiation; tumours of undifferentiated cells are anaplastic, a reliable indicator of malignancy. Good differentiation does not exclude malignancy; anaplasia essentially confirms it. Grading (well / moderately / poorly differentiated) is based on it.

Dysplasia sits between: disordered but not yet malignant growth, with architectural and cellular atypia confined by the basement membrane. Carcinoma in situ = full-thickness dysplasia without invasion.

Oral epithelial dysplasia — sixteen features

Architectural (organisation of the epithelium)Cellular (individual cells)
Irregular epithelial maturation · loss of polarity of basal cells · drop-shaped rete ridges · increased mitotic figures · abnormally superficial mitotic figures · premature keratinisation in single cells · keratin pearls within rete ridges · loss of epithelial cell cohesionAbnormal variation in nuclear size and shape · abnormal variation in cell size and shape · increased nuclear–cytoplasmic ratio · atypical mitotic figures · increased number and size of nucleoli · nuclear hyperchromatism

Mitosis is normally confined to the basal layer, with cells maturing and losing the ability to divide as they move up; a mitotic figure high in the epithelium means maturation control has been lost. Graded mild (lower third), moderate (to middle third), severe (upper third) — the "degree of dysplasia" that Lecture 6 correlated with candidal carriage (Ch 1), and what the pathologist is counting in a biopsied leukoplakia.

Clinical effects of neoplasms

Benign — harm by position and functionMalignant — all of those, plus invasion
Pressure on adjacent tissue — a benign meningeal tumour causing epilepsy · obstruction of flow — a benign epithelial tumour blocking a duct (salivary), airway, bowel · hormone production — a thyroid adenoma causing thyrotoxicosis, a pituitary adenoma · transformation into a malignant neoplasm — adenomatous polyp → adenocarcinoma · anxiety — the patient fears something sinister, a reason to investigate promptly · also haemorrhage, infection, torsionPressure on and destruction of adjacent tissue · metastases — the defining effect · blood loss from ulcerated surfaces (anaemia) · obstruction — colonic tumour causing intestinal obstruction · hormone production — ACTH and ADH from lung tumours · other paraneoplastic effects — weight loss, debility · anxiety and pain · nerve involvement (paraesthesia of the lip in a mandibular malignancy)

"Benign" does not mean harmless — location and secretion matter as much as behaviour, which is why benign lesions in confined spaces (skull, duct, airway) are treated seriously.

Cachexia and paraneoplastic syndromes

Cancer cachexia: progressive loss of body fat and lean body mass with profound weakness, anorexia and anaemia — driven by cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-6) and raised metabolic rate, not simply by the tumour's consumption. A paraneoplastic syndrome is a symptom complex in a cancer patient that cannot be explained by local or distant spread, or by hormones indigenous to the tissue of origin. Commonest: hypercalcaemia (PTHrP from squamous carcinomas), Cushing syndrome (ectopic ACTH from small-cell lung cancer), non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (hypercoagulability); also SIADH, myasthenic syndromes, dermatomyositis, clubbing. They matter because they may be the earliest manifestation of an occult neoplasm, may be lethal in themselves, and may mimic metastatic disease and confound treatment. A lung tumour making ADH qualifies (lung does not make ADH); a thyroid tumour making thyroxine does not.

Epidemiology

The lecture presents worldwide age-standardised incidence and mortality, age-specific rates by sex, five-year survival trends (1984–88 to 2009–13), the top ten cancer sites worldwide and the most common Australian cancers. Take from the graphs: incidence and mortality maps differ — high-income regions record more incidence, lower-income regions have a worse mortality-to-incidence ratio (detection and treatment access, not just biology); incidence rises steeply with age, consistent with the multistep accumulation of mutations; and five-year survival has improved substantially. Lip, oral cavity and pharyngeal cancers do not top the lists but are cancers a dentist is uniquely placed to detect early.

Carcinogens and host factors

The oral and pharyngeal carcinogens are treated in full in Chapter 4.

Classes of carcinogenHost factors
Chemicals (tobacco PAHs and nitrosamines, alcohol/acetaldehyde, aromatic amines, asbestos) · viruses (HPV, EBV, HHV-8, HBV/HCV) · ionising and non-ionising radiation (X-rays, UV) · exogenous hormones (oestrogens) · microbial agents (H. pylori, chronic candidal inflammation)Race · diet · constitutional factors (sex, age, inherited risk — BRCA, retinoblastoma, familial polyposis) · premalignant lesions and conditions (leukoplakia, erythroplakia, oral submucous fibrosis, lichen planus, chronic hyperplastic candidosis, syphilitic leukoplakia, actinic cheilitis) · transplacental exposure · immunosuppression · P450 polymorphisms and DNA-repair capacity

Carcinogenesis needs both columns: the same exposure produces cancer in one person and not another. The carcinogen supplies the insult; the host determines how it is metabolised, how well the damage is repaired, and whether a transformed cell survives immune surveillance.

Drill

Define neoplasia and give three microscopic and three macroscopic features distinguishing benign from malignant.

A neoplasm is an abnormal, autonomous growth of cells that persists in the absence of the initiating stimulus. Microscopic: mitoses (few and normal vs frequent and atypical); differentiation (good vs variable to anaplastic); nuclei (normal vs enlarged, hyperchromatic, pleomorphic, high N:C ratio with prominent nucleoli). Macroscopic: border (circumscribed/encapsulated vs poorly defined, infiltrative); surface growth (exophytic vs endophytic, ulcerated, indurated); necrosis and haemorrhage (rare vs common). Absolute discriminators: invasion and metastasis.

Describe tumour nomenclature with examples of each category.

Benign: tissue root + -oma — lipoma, chondroma, adenoma, squamous papilloma, haemangioma, leiomyoma. Malignant epithelial: carcinoma — squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma (glandular), basal cell carcinoma. Malignant mesenchymal: sarcoma — liposarcoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma. Exceptions ending in -oma but malignant: lymphoma, melanoma, mesothelioma, seminoma. Embryonal: -blastoma.

Why can a paraneoplastic syndrome complicate treatment rather than just accompany it?

Because it may mimic metastatic disease — hypercalcaemia or unexplained systemic illness can suggest widespread spread and push management toward palliation when the primary is still curable. It may also be the first sign of an occult tumour, and may itself be lethal.

A pedunculated pink lump on the gingiva vs an indurated ulcer with rolled margins on the lateral tongue. Which features push each toward benign or malignant, and what do you do?

The pedunculated exophytic lump with a defined border is the benign growth pattern (fibroma, papilloma, pyogenic granuloma). The endophytic, indurated, rolled-margin ulcer is the malignant pattern — likely SCC. Induration means infiltration into stroma. Both need a diagnosis, but the tongue lesion needs urgent biopsy and neck examination; a persistent lesion of more than 2–3 weeks is biopsied regardless of appearance.

Chapter 3 · Tutorial 7B

Neoplasia 2 — Pathogenesis & Hallmarks

How a cell becomes autonomous: genes, epigenetics, the eight hallmarks and viral shortcuts

Chapter 2 described what a neoplasm looks like; this chapter explains how it comes to exist. Cancer is a disease of accumulated genetic and epigenetic change in a single cell lineage, and Hanahan and Weinberg's hallmarks are the framework that organises every mechanism.

Know these cold

  • Tumourigenesis = neoplastic transformation driven by genetic and epigenetic alterations; malignant transformation adds invasion and metastasis
  • Initiation (carcinogen induces mutation) → promotion (clonal proliferation) → progression (malignant behaviour)
  • Tumour suppressors need two hits (recessive); oncogenes need one (dominant) — p53 dominant-negative is the exception
  • p53 (17p): G1 arrest and repair, or apoptosis; mutated in >70% of cancers. RB gates G1/S
  • Eight hallmarks + two enablers (genomic instability, tumour-promoting inflammation)
  • No tumour exceeds 1–2 mm without angiogenesis
  • HPV E6 → p53, E7 → pRb — Hallmark 2 acquired by infection, not mutation

Neoplastic transformation

Neoplastic transformation (tumourigenesis) is the process by which a normal cell acquires the genetic and epigenetic alterations that make its growth autonomous — a single cell gains a survival and proliferation advantage and founds a clone. Two kinds of change:

Genetic alterationsEpigenetic changes
Point mutations (nonsense, missense), deletions, insertions, translocations (BCR-ABL, MYC–IgH), rearrangements, amplifications (HER2, MYC), aneuploidy. The sequence is changed — permanent and heritable through division.Promoter methylation silencing transcription, histone modification, microRNA dysregulation. The DNA sequence is unchanged but the gene is switched off or on — reversible in principle, invisible to sequencing.

Malignant transformation is the further acquisition of invasion and metastasis. Neoplastic transformation makes a cell autonomous; malignant transformation adds spread. A benign neoplasm has undergone the first without the second — which is why some benign lesions later progress, as an adenomatous polyp does to adenocarcinoma.

Tutorial 7B MCQ 1: tumourigenesis is primarily driven by b) genetic and epigenetic alterations.

Initiation, promotion, progression

  1. InitiationA carcinogen induces the genetic alteration(s) that give the transformed cell its neoplastic potential — irreversible but silent; the initiated cell looks normal. Chemical (tobacco PAHs → DNA adducts), radiation (UV dimers, X-ray breaks), viral (integration).
  2. PromotionStimulation of clonal proliferation of the initiated cell — promoters are not themselves mutagenic (hormones, chronic inflammation, alcohol, repeated irritation, phorbol esters); the effect is reversible and requires repeated, prolonged exposure; proliferation fixes the mutation and exposes the clone to further hits.
  3. ProgressionThe process culminating in malignant behaviour — further mutations, genomic instability, heterogeneity, selection of aggressive subclones, invasion, metastasis, drug resistance. Benign → malignant (adenoma → carcinoma).
ClonalOriginating from a single cell transformed by cumulative mutational events — every cell in the tumour inherits the founder's alterations, which is what makes molecular markers and targeted therapy possible
PolyclonalOriginating from multiple cells (hyperplasia, reactive lesions)
CarcinogenAn environmental agent participating in the causation of tumours
Multistep carcinogenesisThe hypothesis that cancer requires an accumulation of several successive changes, not one — explaining latency, age-dependence and the adenoma–carcinoma sequence
Tutorial 7B MCQ 2: initiation = c) induction of genetic alterations by a carcinogen.

Three genetic routes to a transformed cell

RouteWhat happensGenetics
Oncogene activationActivation or abnormal expression of oncogenes — an accelerator stuck onOne activated allele is enough — dominant at cell level (gain of function)
Loss of a tumour suppressorLoss or inactivation of both copies — a brake removedBoth copies must be lost — recessive at cell level, the double-hit model (loss of function)
Expression of telomeraseRestores the ability to divide indefinitely (Hallmark 5)Re-expression of a normally silent enzyme

Brakes must both fail; one stuck accelerator is enough. Add the genes of apoptosis (BCL2 up, BAX down) and DNA repair (genomic instability) as the supporting cast.

Tumour suppressor genes

The double-hit model: the first hit is the acquired mutational loss, or inheritance of a defective allele, of a tumour suppressor gene — the other, wild-type allele still expresses sufficient suppressive effect. The second hit is acquired loss of the normal allele, fully depriving the cell of suppression. Someone born with one defective allele carries the first hit in every cell and needs only one further event in any single cell — which is why familial cancers present earlier, bilaterally and multifocally (retinoblastoma, familial adenomatous polyposis/APC, BRCA1/2, Li–Fraumeni/TP53, NF1).

Caretaker genesGatekeeper genes
Maintain the integrity of the genome by repairing DNA damage — mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2), BRCA1/2, ATM, XP genes. Lose them and mutations accumulate.Inhibit proliferation or promote death of cells with damaged DNA — RB, p53, p16, APC, PTEN. Lose them and mutated cells are permitted to divide.
Tutorial 7B MCQ 3: the double-hit model is most relevant to c) tumour suppressor gene inactivation.

p53 — guardian of the genome

On the short arm of chromosome 17; the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer — defective in more than 70% of cancers, with the remainder often having defects upstream or downstream. Normally it senses DNA damage and (1) arrests the cycle in G1 (via p21) until damage is repaired before S phase, (2) drives senescence, or (3) induces apoptosis (via BAX, PUMA) if damage is extensive. Loss lets DNA-damaged cells survive and replicate (midterm Ch 2).

Mechanism of p53 lossDetail
MutationNonsense (unreadable) or missense (defective or altered-function protein); Li–Fraumeni syndrome inherits one mutant allele
Dominant-negative complexesMutant p53 forms complexes with normal p53 in heterozygous cells and inactivates or subverts it — one mutated allele can suffice; the explicit exception to the two-hit model
Viral protein bindingNormal p53 bound and degraded by proteins of oncogenic DNA viruses — HPV E6, polyomaviruses; the gene is normal, the protein is neutralised
MDM2 amplificationExcess of the protein that degrades p53

Genomic instability

Cells that have lost the mechanisms for sensing and repairing DNA damage have genomic instability — an enabling characteristic that accelerates accumulation of the mutations that actually drive growth. Chromosomal instability (breaks — Fanconi anaemia, ataxia telangiectasia); microsatellite instability from defective mismatch repair (HNPCC/Lynch syndrome — familial carcinoma of caecum and proximal colon, also endometrium); xeroderma pigmentosum — autosomal recessive nucleotide-excision repair defect, greatly increased cancer in sun-exposed skin.

Oncogenes

Oncogenes are genes driving the neoplastic behaviour of cells, derived from normal proto-oncogenes by gain of function. Two routes to activation: an altered protein that is excessively active (point mutation — RAS), or too much normal protein (amplification — HER2, MYC; translocation to an active promoter — BCR-ABL, MYC–IgH in Burkitt; viral insertion). Detected as more oncoprotein, more mRNA, or increased gene copy number.

Class (following the signalling pathway)Example oncogeneProduct / cancer
Growth factorssisPDGF β-chain — astrocytoma, osteosarcoma
Growth-factor receptorserbB1/2 (EGFR, HER2), RETLung, head-and-neck SCC; breast; MEN2
Membrane tyrosine kinasesrc, ABLBCR-ABL in CML — target of imatinib
Signal transducer (GTP-binding)RAS (K-, H-, N-)Commonest oncogene mutation — colon, pancreas, lung; locked GTP-bound "on"
Nuclear transcription factorsMYC, JUN, FOSBurkitt lymphoma (t(8;14)), neuroblastoma (N-MYC amplification)
Cell-cycle regulatorsCyclin D, CDK4Mantle-cell lymphoma, melanoma
Anti-apoptoticBCL2Follicular lymphoma (t(14;18))

Normal proliferation, which oncogenes hijack at any step: growth factor binds its receptor → transient and limited receptor activation → signal-transducing proteins on the inner membrane → transmission across the cytosol → nuclear regulatory factors initiate transcription and biosynthesis → cell-cycle entry. Cancer converts "transient" into continuous — which is Hallmark 1.

Epigenetic contributions

MechanismEffect
Promoter hypermethylationSilencing of tumour suppressors by methylation of CpG islands (p16, MLH1, BRCA1) — intact but unread; as unprotected as if deleted, invisible to sequencing, and reversible (demethylating drugs)
Histone modificationMethylation, acetylation, phosphorylation — the "histone code" opening or closing chromatin (HDAC inhibitors)
microRNAShort inhibitory RNA: more miRNA degrades mRNA and reduces expression (oncomiRs silencing suppressors); less miRNA enhances expression of oncogenes
Copy-number changeTo enhancer and regulatory regions

The hallmarks of cancer

Hanahan and Weinberg (2000, 2011): the acquired capabilities that every cancer must gain, however it gets them, plus two enabling characteristics that make acquiring them easier.

#HallmarkIn one lineMechanism
1Self-sufficiency in growth signalsMakes its own acceleratorGain-of-function oncogenes: own growth factors or stromal induction; overexpressed/mutant receptors; downstream RAS/RAF/PI3K; continuous MYC; CDK4/cyclin D gain, CDKI loss
2Insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signalsIgnores the brakesLoss of RB (G1/S gate), TP53, p16, TGF-β pathway, APC; loss of contact inhibition (midterm Ch 5)
3Altered cellular metabolismRefuels for buildingWarburg effect — aerobic glycolysis to lactate despite oxygen, supplying carbon skeletons for synthesis; a consequence of the same deregulated signalling as 1 and 2 (basis of PET-FDG imaging)
4Evasion of cell deathRefuses to dieBCL2 up, BAX/PUMA down, p53 out; disabled intrinsic pathway; CD95/Fas down
5Unlimited replicative potentialNever ages outTelomerase re-expression avoids senescence and mitotic catastrophe (~90% of cancers)
6Sustained angiogenesisBuilds its own supply linesNo solid tumour can exceed 1–2 mm without inducing angiogenesis — balance tipped to promoters (VEGF, FGF, hypoxia/HIF-1) over inhibitors (thrombospondin); uses the wound-healing machinery of midterm Ch 5; anti-VEGF drugs
7Invasion and metastasisLeaves homeLoosening (E-cadherin loss) → matrix degradation (MMPs) → migration → intravasation → survival in circulation → extravasation → colonisation. Site set by anatomy/vascular drainage (colon → liver) and tropism (prostate → bone). The major cause of morbidity and death
8Evasion of immune surveillanceHides from the immune systemAntigenic yet tolerated: loss of MHC I, immunosuppressive cytokines (TGF-β), regulatory T cells, and checkpoint ligands — PD-L1 on tumour cells switching off T cells; checkpoint-blocking antibodies (anti-PD-1/PD-L1, anti-CTLA-4) release the brake
+Genomic instabilityEnablerMutation accumulates faster — HNPCC, XP, p53 loss
+Tumour-promoting inflammationEnablerInflammatory cells supply growth factors, remove growth suppressors, resist death, drive angiogenesis, invasion and immune evasion — six of the eight hallmarks from outside the tumour cell; why chronic inflammation is a cancer risk
Tutorial 7B MCQ 4 (angiogenesis): c) it provides tumours with a nutrient and oxygen supply beyond a certain size.

Hallmarks 1 and 2 in the cell cycle

Two main checkpoints — G1/S and G2/M — each balanced by growth-promoting and growth-suppressing factors and by DNA-damage sensors. RB is the key negative regulator of the G1/S checkpoint, the portal through which cells must pass before DNA replication: hypophosphorylated RB binds and silences the transcription factor E2F; growth signals raise cyclin D–CDK4/6, which phosphorylate RB, release E2F and commit the cell to S phase; growth inhibitors (TGF-β, p16, contact inhibition) act by keeping RB active. At least one of p16, cyclin D, CDK4 or RB is mutated in most human cancers. p53-mediated arrest is the primordial response to DNA damage, acting through the same gate (p21 inhibits CDKs, keeping RB active).

Tutorial 7B scenario — RB1 mutation. Loss of RB frees E2F permanently: the cell enters S phase without needing external growth factors (Hallmark 1) and cannot respond to TGF-β, p16 or contact inhibition, all of which act through RB (Hallmark 2). Additional cell-cycle mutations (cyclin D/CDK4 gain, p16 or p53 loss) reinforce both and disable the damage checkpoint, so further mutations accumulate.

Targeted therapy follows from the framework: knowing which hallmark a tumour has acquired and how lets treatment aim at a receptor (trastuzumab), a kinase (imatinib), a vessel (bevacizumab) or an immune checkpoint, rather than at dividing cells in general as cytotoxic chemotherapy does.

Viral carcinogenesis

Virus typeMechanismExamples
Oncogenic DNA virusViral DNA integrates into host DNA; viral oncogenes are expressed — HPV E6 binds and degrades p53, E7 binds and inactivates pRb — disabling both gatekeepers without mutating either geneHPV-16/18 (cervical, oropharyngeal), EBV (Burkitt and other lymphomas, nasopharyngeal ca, hairy leukoplakia), HHV-8 (Kaposi's), HBV, Merkel-cell polyomavirus
"Acute" transforming RNA retrovirusRetroviral RNA has picked up a transcribed copy of a cellular oncogene from a prior host; reverse transcribed and integrated, the viral genome now carries a viral oncogene (v-src, v-ras) — brings its own acceleratorRous sarcoma virus (animal)
"Slow" transforming RNA retrovirusCarries no oncogene; inserts its promoter/enhancer next to a cellular oncogene and over-expresses it — stands on the accelerator you already hadFeline leukaemia virus, avian leukosis virus. (HTLV-1, which causes adult T-cell leukaemia, works by a third route — its Tax protein trans-activates host genes — rather than by insertion)

Squamous papilloma — HPV-6/11 — is the benign end of the same spectrum: an exophytic, pedunculated, cauliflower-like lesion, not premalignant, treated by conservative excision. High-risk HPV-16 in the oropharynx (tonsil, base of tongue, presenting as a neck node) is the malignant end, the only oral-region carcinogen with a vaccine.

Drill

Why does a tumour suppressor need both copies lost, but an oncogene only one activated allele?

A suppressor is a brake: one functioning allele still makes enough protein to hold the cell, so both must be lost — recessive at the cellular level, the double-hit model. An oncogene is an accelerator: one constitutively active allele makes an always-on protein whose signal the normal allele cannot cancel — dominant. Exception on the suppressor side: dominant-negative mutant p53 poisons the normal protein, so one hit can suffice.

Define tumourigenesis and explain how genetic and epigenetic alterations contribute.

Neoplastic transformation is the acquisition, in a single cell lineage, of heritable alterations that make growth autonomous. Genetic alterations change the sequence — activating oncogenes (RAS point mutation, MYC amplification, BCR-ABL translocation) or inactivating tumour suppressors (RB, TP53 deletion/mutation) — and are fixed by clonal proliferation. Epigenetic alterations change expression without changing sequence — promoter hypermethylation silencing p16 or MLH1, histone modification, miRNA dysregulation — with the same functional effect, reversible and invisible to sequencing. Together they satisfy the hallmarks through the multistep sequence of initiation, promotion and progression.

A solid tumour has every mutation needed for malignancy but stays at 2 mm. What is missing?

Angiogenesis. Beyond 1–2 mm diffusion cannot supply oxygen and nutrients to the centre; growth resumes only when the balance of promoters (VEGF, FGF, driven by hypoxia) over inhibitors is tipped and new vessels are recruited from the stroma.

How does an oncogenic DNA virus cause cancer without mutating any host gene?

Its genome integrates and expresses viral oncogenes whose products bind the host's tumour-suppressor proteins: HPV E6 inactivates p53 and E7 inactivates pRb. The host genes are structurally normal; their proteins are neutralised, so the G1/S gate and the DNA-damage response are both lost — Hallmark 2 by infection.

Tutorial 7B — answer key

MCQ — tumourigenesis is primarily driven by
b) Genetic and epigenetic alterations.
MCQ — initiation phase involves
c) Induction of genetic alterations by a carcinogen.
MCQ — double-hit model is most relevant to
c) Tumour suppressor gene inactivation.
MCQ — role of angiogenesis
c) Provides a nutrient and oxygen supply beyond a certain size (1–2 mm).
SAQ — define tumourigenesis; genetic and epigenetic contributions
Acquisition of heritable alterations conferring autonomous growth in one clone. Genetic: oncogene gain of function (mutation, amplification, translocation), suppressor loss (two hits), telomerase, repair-gene loss. Epigenetic: promoter hypermethylation, histone code, miRNA — expression changed without sequence change; reversible.
SAQ — three phases of multistep carcinogenesis
Initiation: carcinogen induces irreversible mutation in a cell. Promotion: non-mutagenic promoter stimulates clonal proliferation of the initiated cell; reversible, needs repeated exposure. Progression: further mutations/genomic instability → heterogeneity, invasion, metastasis — malignant behaviour.
Scenario — RB1 mutation and Hallmarks 1 & 2
RB gates G1/S by binding E2F. Loss releases E2F permanently: S-phase entry without growth factors (self-sufficiency) and no response to TGF-β, p16, contact inhibition which act through RB (insensitivity to inhibition). Other cell-cycle mutations (cyclin D/CDK4 gain, p16/p53 loss) compound both and disable damage arrest.
