Chapter 4 · Lecture 7C

Carcinogens of Lip, Oral Cavity & Pharyngeal Cancer

Aetiological agents, how they act, how they combine, and how risk is reversed

Chapter 3 described the machinery of carcinogenesis — initiation, promotion, progression and the hallmarks. This chapter names the agents that drive that machinery in the mouth and pharynx, and adds the single most useful clinical idea in oral cancer prevention: risks multiply, and they fall when exposure stops.

Know these cold

  • LOPC is multifactorial: behavioural, infectious, environmental/occupational and host factors
  • Tobacco is the dominant carcinogen; tobacco-specific nitrosamines (NNK, NNN) are the most significant; DNA adducts and p53 overexpression
  • Alcohol → acetaldehyde via alcohol dehydrogenase; it also makes mucosa more permeable to other carcinogens
  • Tobacco + alcohol is multiplicative: 6–15× above either alone; ~30× for heavy smoking + heavy drinking vs neither
  • Betel quid / areca nut is carcinogenic independently of tobacco and alcohol
  • HPV 16 → E6 inhibits p53, E7 inactivates pRb; the only major carcinogen here with a vaccine
  • UV is the principal cause of lower-lip cancer
  • Duration of smoking matters more than daily count; risk approaches never-smoker baseline ~20 years after quitting

A multifactorial disease

Lip, oral cavity and pharyngeal cancers (LOPC) arise from cumulative carcinogen exposure across several independent and interacting pathways — almost all of them squamous cell carcinoma. The lecture groups the causes into four:

PathwayAgents
BehaviouralTobacco (smoked and smokeless), betel quid, alcohol, e-cigarettes
Infectious / biologicalHPV 16/18, the oral microbiome, chronic inflammation
Environmental / occupationalUV radiation; wood and asbestos dust; formaldehyde
Host and lifestyleGenetic polymorphisms, diet, socioeconomic access
Map these onto Ch 2's two columns: the first three rows are carcinogens; the fourth is host factors. Ch 3's sequence tells you what each does — tobacco initiates (DNA adducts), chronic inflammation and alcohol largely promote, and continued exposure drives progression.

Tobacco smoking — the dominant carcinogen

Cigarette smoke contains more than 60 carcinogens; the tobacco-specific nitrosamines are the most significant.

Key carcinogen classNote
Tobacco-specific nitrosaminesNNK (nicotine-derived nitrosamine ketone) and NNN (N′-nitrosonornicotine) — formed from nicotine during curing and burning
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbonsProducts of incomplete combustion, e.g. benzo[a]pyrene
Nicotine metabolitesNicotine itself is addictive rather than the main carcinogen; its derivatives are
DNA-adduct-forming agentsThe common final mechanism

Mechanism

The carcinogens form DNA adducts — chemical groups bonded covalently to DNA bases. If an adduct is not repaired before the cell replicates, the base is misread and a permanent mutation results: this is initiation. Smokers' premalignant and malignant oral epithelium shows p53 overexpression (mutant p53 accumulates because it is not degraded) — the guardian of the genome from Ch 3, disabled.

Dose, duration and reversibility

  • A clear dose–response: heavier and longer exposure confers greater risk (e.g. more than 2 packs a day ≈ 3.8× the risk of recurrence).
  • Risk rises disproportionately with intensity, not linearly.
  • Duration matters most: just 7 years of smoking roughly doubles risk (RR 2.01).
  • Excess risk persists for decades after stopping, but largely resolves by about 20 years after quitting.
Smoking statusOral cavity riskPharyngeal riskMortality risk
Never-smoker1.00 (baseline)1.001.00
Light (6 cigarettes/day)1.98×1.98×Elevated
Moderate (10/day)2.88×2.88×Substantially increased
Heavy (20/day)4.78×4.78×High
Former smoker1.41×1.94×Elevated

Overall, current smokers carry 3.58× the risk (3.39× oral cavity, 4.24× pharyngeal), and a 7.86× mortality; former smokers still have 1.61× mortality.

Smokeless tobacco and betel quid

Smokeless tobaccoBetel quid / areca nut
Naswar, gutka, khaini, zarda, toombak, shammah — nicotine content varies widely (0.8–76 mg/g). Contains PAHs, nitrosamines and radioactive polonium-210. Users absorb 2–3× more nicotine than smokers. About 4× higher oral cancer risk than non-users in South-East Asia. Held in the buccal sulcus, so cancers arise where the quid sits.Areca nut + slaked lime, with or without tobacco, wrapped in a betel leaf. Risk is independent of concurrent tobacco or alcohol use — the areca nut is a carcinogen in its own right. Arecoline activates epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) markers such as vimentin in oral epithelium. Highest incidence in South and South-East Asia and the Pacific Islands. Also causes oral submucous fibrosis, a potentially malignant disorder.
EMT is the loosening step of Hallmark 7 (Ch 3): epithelial cells lose E-cadherin and gain mesenchymal features such as vimentin, which lets them migrate and invade.

Alcohol — carcinogen and cofactor

  1. AcetaldehydeEthanol is converted to acetaldehyde, a known carcinogen, by alcohol dehydrogenase — in the liver, and in the mouth by oral bacteria and mucosa. The lecture describes acetaldehyde as a tumour promoter; it also forms DNA adducts.
  2. Slow clearance in some peopleAcetaldehyde is cleared by aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2). About 44% of Japanese people carry an inactive ALDH2 variant, which prolongs exposure (and causes facial flushing after drinking).
  3. Solvent effectAlcohol increases oral mucosal permeability, helping other carcinogens penetrate — this is how it amplifies tobacco.

Synergy, not addition

Combined tobacco and alcohol use raises oral cancer risk 6–15× above either exposure alone — the effect is multiplicative, not additive. Alcohol alone carries an odds ratio of about 3.8; alcohol + tobacco + betel raises it to about 27.5. And for the extremes: heavy smoking combined with heavy drinking carries roughly 30× the risk of neither habit.

Why multiplicative? Alcohol dissolves and carries tobacco carcinogens through the mucosa, adds its own acetaldehyde, and (as a promoter) drives proliferation of cells the tobacco has already mutated. Each agent makes the other more effective.

E-cigarettes — an emerging exposure

Assessed against the Bradford Hill criteria for causation (Raj et al., 2020) — strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy:

Lower toxicant loadSubstantially fewer carcinogens than combustible smoke — but not zero
DNA strand breaksOccur in oral cell lines regardless of nicotine content (Yu et al.)
Gene dysregulation62% of dysregulated oral-epithelium transcripts are linked to cancer pathways (Tommasi et al.)
Causation unprovenNo long-term prospective data; case reports of OSCC in e-cigarette-only users exist

The honest summary: biologically plausible, probably less harmful than smoking, and not proven to be safe. Temporality and biological gradient — the Bradford Hill criteria that need decades of follow-up — are exactly what is missing.

HPV — a viral carcinogen

  • HPV-16 (then HPV-18) is the dominant oncogenic type in the head and neck.
  • Viral E6 inhibits p53; E7 binds and inactivates pRb — disabling the two key tumour-suppressor checkpoints without mutating either gene (Ch 3).
  • Tonsil and base-of-tongue tissue are preferentially infected — up to 94% positivity in oropharyngeal SCC.
  • The attributable fraction of oropharyngeal cancer is about 18–28% globally, and up to ~70% in the United States.

HPV is the only major oral-cavity/oropharyngeal carcinogen with a preventive vaccine; vaccine effectiveness against HPV-16/18 reaches about 82% at 6 years.

HPV status changes risk: among HPV-negative smokers the relative risk is 3.28, versus 1.35 in HPV-positive smokers, in whom viral mechanisms dominate. HPV-positive and HPV-negative tumours are, in effect, different diseases.

Ch 1 gives the epidemiology: 40–80% of oropharyngeal cancers are HPV-positive and 90% of those are HPV 16, but only ~3.6% of oral cavity cancers.

Environmental and occupational carcinogens

ExposureEffect
UV radiationThe principal cause of lower-lip cancer; higher risk in fishermen, farmers and gardeners (standardised incidence ratio up to 2.26). The lower lip faces the sun; the upper lip is shaded. Precursor: actinic cheilitis
Occupational dustsWood, cement, coal and asbestos dust — wood dust raises oropharyngeal risk 2–5×
Chemical exposuresFormaldehyde, chromium (leather dust) and metal particles — linked to pharyngeal and nasopharyngeal cancer

Diet, oral microbiome and host susceptibility

Diet and the oral microbiomeGenetic and familial susceptibility
High red and processed meat with low fruit and vegetable intake raises risk; Mediterranean-pattern diets are protective. Processed-meat carcinogens: heterocyclic amines, PAHs and haem-iron-driven N-nitroso compounds. Poor oral hygiene and periodontal pathogens (e.g. P. gingivalis) promote chronic inflammation and leukoplakia — and let tobacco carcinogens linger in the mouth.Polymorphisms in P450/xenobiotic-metabolising enzymes change how carcinogens are activated and detoxified, and how well DNA is repaired. ADH1B/ADH7 variants alter acetaldehyde exposure. p53/pRb inactivation drives genomic instability. A first-degree relative with LOPC increases risk independent of shared tobacco and alcohol exposure.
This is why two people with identical smoking histories have different outcomes: the same carcinogen is metabolised, repaired and survived differently (Ch 2, "Carcinogens and host factors").

Epigenetics and socioeconomic drivers

Environmental, genetic and epigenetic inputs, together with ageing, converge on epigenetic regulation — DNA methylation, histone modification and post-transcriptional gene silencing by microRNAs (the mechanisms in Ch 3, "Epigenetic contributions"). In low- and middle-income settings, risk habits, poor oral-health literacy, low education and limited awareness compound the biological risk, and economic burden both results from and perpetuates delayed diagnosis and higher-risk exposure.

Putting it together: risk/epigenetic factors (alcohol, betel quid, diet, tobacco) + environmental factors (viral, fungal and bacterial infection; occupational exposure; poor oral health) + host factors (age, genetics). Carcinogenesis is the cumulative product of overlapping exposures — not any single agent.

Reversing the risk

Years since quitting smokingRisk reduction
1–4 years≈35% lower
5 years≈50% lower
10 yearsA further ≈50% lower
20+ yearsBack to never-smoker baseline

Total duration smoked matters more than daily cigarette count — quitting early avoids the steep rise after 7–10 years. Two modifiers from the same slide: poor oral hygiene lets tobacco carcinogens linger in the mouth, intensifying exposure; and in Oceania the relative risk for smokers reaches 6.44, well above the global average.

The quit timeline is the evidence behind brief smoking-cessation advice in the dental chair — a patient who quits now still gains most of the benefit.

Prevention targets the carcinogens

LevelAimMeasures
PrimaryStop the cancer startingTobacco and alcohol cessation, HPV vaccination, sun protection, dietary modification
SecondaryFind it earlyRoutine dental screening, visual and tactile examination, biomarkers, chemoprevention in leukoplakia
TertiaryLimit the damage of established diseaseStructured follow-up, rehabilitation, and management of field cancerisation (the whole carcinogen-exposed mucosa is at risk of a second primary)

Key takeaways (the lecture's own six)

  1. MultifactorialBehavioural, infectious, environmental and host factors interact and compound.
  2. Tobacco dominatesRisk scales with both intensity and duration of use.
  3. SynergySmoking with heavy alcohol use raises risk roughly 30-fold — synergistic, not additive.
  4. HPV is vaccine-preventableThe only major carcinogen here with a preventive vaccine.
  5. Quitting worksExcess risk falls within years and approaches baseline by ~20 years smoke-free.
  6. Prevention at every levelPrimary, secondary and tertiary prevention all reduce the burden.

Sources cited on the slides: Ebrahimi et al. 2025 (Health Science Reports); Irani 2020 (International Journal of Preventive Medicine); Raj et al. 2020 (Translational Cancer Research).

Drill

Explain why combined tobacco and alcohol use multiplies oral cancer risk rather than simply adding to it.

Tobacco supplies the initiating carcinogens — nitrosamines and PAHs that form DNA adducts and cause mutations. Alcohol acts on the same tissue in three ways: it increases mucosal permeability so the tobacco carcinogens penetrate further; it is converted to acetaldehyde, itself carcinogenic and promoting; and it encourages proliferation of already-initiated cells. Each exposure raises the effectiveness of the other, so the combined risk (6–15× above either alone; ~30× for heavy use of both vs neither) exceeds the sum.

A 45-year-old fisherman has a crusted, persistent lesion on the lower lip. Which carcinogen, which precursor, and why the lower lip?

Ultraviolet radiation — the principal cause of lower-lip cancer, with higher risk in outdoor workers such as fishermen, farmers and gardeners. The precursor is actinic cheilitis. The lower lip is everted and faces the sun; the upper lip is shaded by the nose and its own angle.

Why is betel quid considered a carcinogen even in people who neither smoke nor drink?

Because epidemiological risk persists after adjusting for tobacco and alcohol — the areca nut is independently carcinogenic. Arecoline activates EMT markers such as vimentin in oral epithelium, and chewing also causes oral submucous fibrosis, a potentially malignant disorder.

A patient asks whether stopping smoking at 50 after 30 years is "too late". What does the evidence say?

No. Risk falls about 35% within 1–4 years, about 50% by 5 years, by a further ~50% at 10 years, and approaches never-smoker baseline after about 20 years. Duration matters more than daily count, so every additional year of smoking avoided is a gain.

How can HPV cause cancer without causing a mutation in p53 or RB?

HPV-16 integrates and expresses E6 and E7. E6 binds and inhibits p53 (promoting its degradation); E7 binds and inactivates pRb, releasing E2F. The host genes are structurally normal but their proteins are neutralised — both the G1/S gate and the DNA-damage response are lost.

Classify these measures as primary, secondary or tertiary prevention: HPV vaccination; examining the lateral tongue at a check-up; surveillance of the remaining mucosa after a resected tongue cancer.

HPV vaccination — primary (prevents the cancer starting). Routine visual and tactile examination — secondary (early detection). Follow-up of field cancerisation after treatment — tertiary (limits recurrence and second primaries).
