Chapter 5 · Lecture 8

Cardiovascular & Blood Disorders

Vessels, heart and haemostasis — and what each means for the patient in the dental chair

Two halves. The first follows a single process — injury to the arterial wall — through atherosclerosis, aneurysm, hypertension, diabetes, ischaemic heart disease and heart failure. The second is haemostasis: how a clot forms and stops, and the disorders that make a patient bleed after an extraction.

Know these cold

  • Atherosclerosis: endothelial injury → LDL enters intima and is oxidised → monocytes → foam cells (fatty streak) → smooth muscle migration → fibrous cap over a necrotic core
  • Vulnerable plaque: thin cap, large lipid core, heavy inflammation (MMPs), little calcium → rupture → thrombosis
  • Hypertension ≥140/90 (clinic), sustained; essential ~90%, secondary ~10%
  • Stable angina: fixed stenosis >70%, exertional, relieved by rest/GTN, troponin normal. MI: necrosis, troponin up, not relieved by GTN
  • Left HF → lungs (dyspnoea, orthopnoea); right HF → body (oedema, hepatomegaly, JVP)
  • Primary haemostasis = platelets + vWF; secondary = coagulation cascade → thrombin → fibrin
  • Vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X. PT/INR = extrinsic; APTT = intrinsic
  • Haemophilia A (FVIII) and B (FIX): X-linked, ↑APTT, normal PT and platelets. vWD: commonest inherited bleeding disorder (~1%)

The arterial wall

Arteries have three layers: intima (endothelium on a thin connective-tissue layer), media (smooth muscle, whose muscularity varies with vessel size) and adventitia, separated by the internal and external elastic laminae. The vasa vasorum supply the outer wall. The endothelium is the critical regulator of vascular health — when intact it is anti-thrombotic and vasodilating (nitric oxide, prostacyclin); when injured it is the starting point of almost every disease in this chapter.

Age-related change — arteriosclerosis

Intimal fibrosisCollagen and matrix accumulate, smooth muscle cells are lost; the intima thickens and stiffens
Medial elastic degenerationElastin fragments and is replaced by dense collagen → reduced compliance and recoil
Arterial stiffeningWidened pulse pressure — systolic rises, diastolic falls in later life → isolated systolic hypertension
Endothelial dysfunctionLess nitric oxide, impaired vasodilation, more pro-inflammatory and pro-thrombotic mediators
Aneurysm riskWeakened media, especially large elastic arteries (abdominal aorta)

Arteriosclerosis is non-inflammatory, age-related arterial hardening — distinct from atherosclerosis, but it contributes to its progression.

Atherosclerosis

Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory, lipid-driven disease of large and medium arteries — elastic and muscular (aorta, coronary, carotid, iliac) — progressive, multifactorial and lifelong. Its central mechanism is endothelial injury + lipid accumulation, with chronic inflammation sustaining plaque growth. Shear stress damages the endothelium most at bifurcations, where flow is turbulent.

Risk factors

FactorHow it acts
AgeCumulative endothelial injury; highest prevalence over 50 (non-modifiable)
Male sexWomen relatively protected before menopause by oestrogen (non-modifiable)
SmokingOxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction
HypertensionMechanical injury; accelerates plaque formation
Diabetes (types 1 and 2)Glycation of proteins, dyslipidaemia, inflammation
HyperlipidaemiaMore LDL available to enter the intima

Pathogenesis — five steps

  1. Endothelial injury / dysfunctionFrom mechanical stress (hypertension), toxins (smoking), hyperglycaemia (diabetes), hyperlipidaemia and turbulent flow.
  2. LDL infiltration and oxidation in the intimaIncreased permeability lets LDL in; oxidised LDL is chemotactic, pro-inflammatory and cytotoxic, and induces adhesion molecules (VCAM-1, ICAM-1) on the endothelium.
  3. Monocytes → macrophages → foam cellsMonocytes adhere and migrate in, become macrophages and engulf oxidised LDL. Lipid-laden foam cells accumulate as fatty streaks and release cytokines that amplify inflammation.
  4. Smooth muscle migration and matrixSmooth muscle cells migrate from the media to the intima and lay down collagen, elastin and proteoglycans.
  5. Fibrous cap over a lipid coreThe cap stabilises the plaque but may thin with time; the necrotic core contains dead cells, cholesterol esters and debris.
This is the midterm's chronic inflammation (Ch 4) with an agent the macrophage cannot remove — oxidised LDL. Foam cells are frustrated macrophages, exactly as in a granuloma.

Fatty streaks are foam-cell-rich and reversible in early life. Atheromatous plaques — a fibrous cap over a necrotic core — are the clinically significant lesion.

Stable versus vulnerable plaque

ComponentRole
Fibrous capCollagen-rich layer made by smooth muscle cells; stabilises the plaque
Lipid-rich necrotic coreCholesterol, cholesterol esters, debris; site of intense inflammation
Foam cells and macrophagesMajor producers of inflammatory cytokines; expand the core
CalcificationProgresses with age; stiffens the vessel
NeovascularisationFragile microvessels → intraplaque haemorrhage

A vulnerable (unstable) plaque has a thin fibrous cap, a large lipid core, a heavy inflammatory infiltrate whose matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) weaken the cap, and little calcification. It is the soft, inflamed plaque — not necessarily the largest — that ruptures.

Clinical consequences

ProcessResult
Progressive stenosis → chronic ischaemiaCoronary → stable angina; peripheral → claudication; mesenteric → post-prandial pain
Plaque rupture → acute thrombosisAcute coronary syndrome; cerebral artery thrombosis → ischaemic stroke; sudden occlusion is life-threatening
Atheroembolism → distal infarctsCholesterol emboli to kidneys, digits, retina — "blue toe syndrome", retinal infarcts, renal impairment
Wall weakening → aneurysmDestruction of the media → dilatation, commonly the abdominal aorta; rupture risk rises with diameter

Aneurysms

An aneurysm is a localised, permanent dilatation of an artery — at least a 50% increase in diameter compared with normal — and represents structural failure of the wall.

TypeCause and site
AtheroscleroticMedial degeneration from plaque-induced ischaemia; usually the abdominal aorta
Dissecting (aortic dissection)An intimal tear lets blood track between the layers of the media; linked to hypertension or connective-tissue disorders
BerryCongenital defects at arterial bifurcations of the circle of Willis; a major cause of subarachnoid haemorrhage
Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysmsHypertensive degeneration of small penetrating cerebral vessels; cause intracerebral haemorrhage
MycoticInfection weakens the wall, often from septic emboli (e.g. infective endocarditis)

Other causes: Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 defect → weak elastic tissue), Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (defective collagen → loss of tensile strength), and vasculitis (e.g. syphilitic aortitis).

Hypertension

Hypertension is persistently elevated arterial blood pressure: ≥140/90 mmHg on clinic readings (home or ambulatory thresholds are slightly lower, ≥135/85, because the white-coat effect is removed). It requires sustained elevation, confirmed across several visits or by 24-hour ambulatory monitoring — not a single reading unless BP is severely raised.

CategorySystolicDiastolic
Optimal<120and<80
Normal120–129and/or80–84
High normal130–139and/or85–89
Grade 1 hypertension140–159and/or90–99
Grade 2 hypertension160–179and/or100–109
Grade 3 hypertension≥180and/or≥110
Isolated systolic hypertension≥140and<90
In the clinic: a single raised reading in a dental chair does not equal a diagnosis — consider anxiety, pain, caffeine and stress, and refer for proper assessment. Elective care is avoided in uncontrolled hypertension; grade 3 (≥180/110) is the usual point at which elective treatment is deferred.

Essential vs secondary

Essential (primary) — ~90%Secondary — ~10%
Multifactorial, with no single identifiable cause. Genetic polymorphisms affecting RAAS, sodium handling and vascular tone. Environmental: high salt, sedentary lifestyle, obesity (→ insulin resistance → sympathetic activation), chronic stress (→ catecholamine excess). Sympathetic overactivity; subclinical renal sodium retention.Renal: chronic kidney disease, renal artery stenosis, polycystic kidney disease. Endocrine: Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism — Na⁺ retention, K⁺ loss), Cushing syndrome (cortisol excess), phaeochromocytoma (catecholamine-secreting tumour — episodic surges), thyroid disease. Cardiovascular: coarctation of the aorta; aortic stiffening. Drugs: NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, ciclosporin, erythropoietin.

Mechanisms of essential hypertension

Blood pressure = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance, and each mechanism raises one or both:

  1. Increased total peripheral resistanceStructural narrowing of small arteries and arterioles; endothelial dysfunction (less NO, more vasoconstriction); vascular remodelling that perpetuates resistance.
  2. Sympathetic overactivityRaised resting heart rate and vasomotor tone; stress-driven catecholamines.
  3. RAAS activationRenin → angiotensin I → angiotensin II (converted by ACE, largely in lung endothelium). Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor and stimulates aldosterone, which retains sodium and water → more blood volume.
  4. Renal sodium retentionImpaired pressure natriuresis — the kidneys need a higher pressure to excrete sodium, causing chronic volume overload.
  5. Genetic predispositionPolymorphisms in ion channels, renin secretion and vascular tone; strong familial aggregation.

Systemic effects — the target organs

OrganDamage
HeartLeft ventricular hypertrophy (concentric, from pressure overload) → more O₂ demand, poor diastolic filling → heart failure; accelerated atherosclerosis; atrial fibrillation
KidneysHypertensive nephrosclerosis — hyaline arteriolosclerosis → glomerular ischaemia → falling GFR → CKD (reduced drug clearance; hyperkalaemia risk with RAAS inhibitors)
BrainLacunar infarcts (small-vessel disease); intracerebral haemorrhage from Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms; vascular dementia
EyesHypertensive retinopathy — arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, cotton-wool spots, haemorrhages; papilloedema in hypertensive emergency
Hypertension is the midterm's hypertrophy (Ch 2) — permanent cardiac myocytes cannot divide, so they enlarge.

Diabetic vascular disease

Diabetes produces three vascular pathologies:

PathologyMechanismConsequencesDental relevance
1. Accelerated atherosclerosis (macrovascular)Glycation of lipoproteins → more LDL oxidation; chronic inflammation from advanced glycation end-products (AGEs); endothelial dysfunctionEarlier, more severe plaques: ischaemic heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease → diabetic foot ulcersPoor perfusion slows healing; higher MI/stroke risk under stress; careful vasoconstrictor use
2. Hypertensive vascular diseaseRenal sodium retention, RAAS overactivity, sympathetic activationLVH, heart failure, renal decline — amplifies 1 and 3Monitor BP; avoid elective care if uncontrolled; adjust doses for renal impairment
3. Diabetic microangiopathy — the hallmarkThickened capillary basement membranes → narrowed lumen; microaneurysms, leakage, haemorrhage, ischaemiaRetina (retinopathy), glomeruli (nephropathy — leading cause of dialysis), vasa nervorum (neuropathy), skin and mucosaPoor wound healing, more infection, altered pain perception

Poor wound healing in diabetes has three causes: reduced perfusion, impaired neutrophil function, and increased infection risk. Autonomic neuropathy can blunt oral pain and cause hypoglycaemia unawareness — relevant when planning sedation.

Retinopathy is a visible marker of widespread microvascular disease — a patient with it carries raised systemic risk.

Vasculitis and giant cell arteritis

Vasculitis is inflammatory destruction of blood-vessel walls, causing weakness, narrowing or occlusion. It is classified by vessel size:

SizeVesselsExamples
LargeAorta and its primary branchesGiant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis
MediumMuscular arteries supplying organsPolyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease
SmallArterioles, capillaries, venulesANCA-associated (granulomatosis with polyangiitis), immune-complex (Henoch–Schönlein purpura), microscopic polyangiitis

Mechanisms: autoimmune (ANCA — PR3 and MPO; T-cell inflammation), immune-complex deposition (post-infectious, SLE — type III hypersensitivity), and infection (hepatitis B/C, bacterial, fungal). Consequences: ischaemia, infarction, aneurysm or rupture, and haemorrhage, purpura or petechiae.

Giant cell (temporal) arteritis

WhoAlmost exclusively over 50; more common in women; associated with polymyalgia rheumatica
HeadacheTemporal, from granulomatous inflammation of the temporal artery; scalp tenderness (pain on brushing hair)
Jaw claudicationPain or fatigue in the jaw muscles during chewing, from ischaemia of masseter and pterygoids — can be mistaken for TMD
EyesAmaurosis fugax, blurred vision, diplopia
SystemicFever, weight loss, malaise
ComplicationIrreversible blindness from occlusion of the ophthalmic artery; stroke; aortic involvement
Red flag for dentists: new jaw pain on chewing in a patient over 50, with headache or visual symptoms, is giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise — same-day medical referral, because sight is at stake.

Heart failure

Heart failure is the inability of the heart to pump sufficient blood to meet metabolic demands — from impaired filling (diastolic dysfunction) or impaired contraction (systolic dysfunction). Neurohormonal activation (sympathetic system, RAAS) then causes fluid retention and venous congestion.

Left-sidedRight-sided
FailureLV cannot pump forward → reduced outputRV cannot pump into the lungs
Backs up intoPulmonary veins → pulmonary congestion and oedemaSystemic veins → oedema and organ congestion
Main causesIschaemic heart disease, hypertension, aortic/mitral valve disease, cardiomyopathyLeft-sided failure (most common), pulmonary hypertension, chronic lung disease (cor pulmonale), pulmonary embolism
SymptomsDyspnoea (exertional → at rest), orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, fatiguePeripheral (pitting) oedema, hepatomegaly, ascites, raised JVP, abdominal discomfort
PathologyPulmonary oedema; haemosiderin-laden "heart failure cells" in the lungsCongested "nutmeg liver"; serous effusions
Dental settingCannot lie flat — treat semi-upright; desaturates in long procedures; sensitive to adrenaline; short, stress-free visits; monitor O₂ saturationReduced hepatic drug clearance (adjust doses); fatigue; positioning around oedema; hypotension when reclined

Congestive heart failure = combined left and right failure, typical of advanced chronic disease. Major causes overall: myocardial infarction, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathies and arrhythmias (e.g. AF).

Ischaemic heart disease

IHD is a mismatch between myocardial oxygen supply and demand. About 90% is caused by coronary atherosclerosis; others include coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal angina) and secondary ischaemia from anaemia, hypotension or tachyarrhythmia. It presents as a spectrum:

Stable anginaUnstable anginaMyocardial infarctionSudden cardiac death
PathologyFixed stenosis (>70% lumen reduction); demand exceeds supply on exertionPlaque rupture + platelet aggregation + non-occlusive thrombusPlaque rupture → complete or near-complete occlusion → irreversible myocyte necrosisFatal arrhythmia (usually VF), often from acute ischaemia
PainPredictable, exertional; relieved by rest or GTNAt rest or minimal exertion; increasing frequency or severitySevere, persistent, >20–30 min; not relieved by GTNOften little or no warning
TroponinNormalNormalRaised—
ECGTransient ST depressionST depression or normalST elevation (STEMI) or depression (NSTEMI); new Q wavesVF / asystole
RiskChronic but stableHigh — pre-infarctionCritical emergencyImmediately fatal
Dental implicationsStress reduction, short visits, GTN availableNo elective care; urgent medical referralLecture: defer elective care for 6 months; bleeding on antiplatelets; high re-infarction riskAED on site, CPR-trained staff, recognise warning signs

GTN works by relaxing vascular smooth muscle: it dilates coronary vessels (more supply) and veins (less preload, so less demand). Rest works by lowering demand. Neither can rescue myocardium whose supply has been cut off by a thrombus — which is why GTN failure suggests infarction. Unstable angina and MI together form the acute coronary syndrome.

Consequences of MI

  • Arrhythmias — ventricular fibrillation is the most common cause of early death
  • Heart failure — loss of contractile tissue lowers the ejection fraction; permanent cardiac muscle is replaced by scar (midterm Ch 5)
  • Cardiogenic shock — severe pump failure → hypotension and organ hypoperfusion
  • Pericarditis — acute fibrinous pericarditis at 1–3 days; Dressler syndrome (autoimmune) weeks later

Sudden cardiac death is unexpected cardiac arrest within 1 hour of symptom onset, usually from VF, triggered by acute ischaemia, structural heart disease or electrical instability. Coronary atherosclerosis is present in most cases, and it may be the first manifestation of IHD.

The lecture's 6-month rule is the traditional teaching; current practice individualises timing after MI in consultation with the patient's cardiologist. For this unit, quote the lecture.

Valvular heart disease and infective endocarditis

CauseEffect
Rheumatic heart diseasePost-streptococcal autoimmune reaction (molecular mimicry — midterm Ch 6–7): leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, chordal shortening; classically the mitral valve, sometimes aortic
Degenerative (calcific)Age-related fibrosis and calcification — the most common cause of aortic stenosis in the elderly
Infective endocarditisLeaflet destruction → acute regurgitation or chronic scarring
CongenitalBicuspid aortic valve (early calcification); mitral valve prolapse

Function fails in two ways: stenosis — the valve cannot open fully → pressure overload → hypertrophy; regurgitation — it cannot close fully → volume overload → dilatation. Rheumatic disease often produces mixed lesions.

Infective endocarditis

DefinitionInfection of the heart valves or endocardial surface
OrganismsViridans streptococci — classically after a dental bacteraemia; Staphylococcus aureus (acute, aggressive); enterococci
High-risk groupsProsthetic valves; previous infective endocarditis; certain congenital heart disease; valve repair with prosthetic material; complex cyanotic heart disease; intravenous drug use (usually right-sided)
ClinicalFever, chills; new or changing murmur; heart failure from valve destruction; embolic phenomena — splinter haemorrhages (nails), Janeway lesions (painless, palms/soles), Osler nodes (tender, fingertips), Roth spots (retinal haemorrhages)
Dental relevance: antibiotic prophylaxis before invasive dental procedures is reserved for the highest-risk groups listed here (in Australian guidelines this also includes rheumatic heart disease in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people). For everyone, good oral health reduces the daily bacteraemia from chewing and brushing, which far exceeds that from occasional procedures.

Mnemonic for the emboli: Osler = Ouch (tender); Janeway = painless; both on hands and feet.

Congenital heart disease

DefectKey points
Ventricular septal defectThe most common congenital defect; left-to-right shunt; pulmonary hypertension if severe
Atrial septal defectOften asymptomatic early; right-heart volume overload
Patent ductus arteriosusPersistence of the fetal ductus; left-to-right shunt; bounding pulses, continuous murmur
Tetralogy of FallotRV outflow obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RV hypertrophy — the classic cyanotic "blue baby" lesion
Left-to-right shuntsRight-to-left shunts
Non-cyanotic — oxygenated blood recirculates through the lungs. Increased pulmonary flow → pulmonary hypertension → Eisenmenger syndrome: the shunt reverses to right-to-left and the patient becomes cyanoticCyanotic — deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation. Chronic hypoxia → polycythaemia and clotting problems (and finger clubbing)

Haemostasis

Haemostasis is a balance: enough clot to stop bleeding, no more. Four components:

  1. Primary haemostasis — the platelet plugInjury exposes subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor (vWF). Platelets adhere via vWF binding to platelet GPIb, then activate — change shape, release granules (ADP, thromboxane A₂, serotonin) and express activated GPIIb/IIIa. Fibrinogen bridges GPIIb/IIIa on neighbouring platelets → aggregation. Result: an unstable, temporary plug.
  2. Secondary haemostasis — the coagulation cascadeAn enzymatic cascade of factors (I–XIII) generates thrombin, which converts fibrinogen → fibrin, stabilising the plug with a mesh.
  3. Natural anticoagulantsAntithrombin (inhibits thrombin and factors Xa, IXa, XIa); protein C + protein S (inactivate factors Va and VIIIa); tissue factor pathway inhibitor. They stop the clot spreading beyond the injury.
  4. FibrinolysisPlasminogen → plasmin via tissue plasminogen activator (tPA); plasmin digests fibrin into fibrin degradation products, removing the clot as repair progresses.

The endothelium is the central regulator: when injured it is pro-coagulant (tissue factor, vWF); when intact it is anti-thrombotic (NO, prostacyclin, thrombomodulin).

The coagulation cascade

PathwayTrigger and factorsLab test
ExtrinsicTissue factor activates factor VII — the rapid responsePT / INR
IntrinsicContact activation → factors XII, XI, IX, VIIIAPTT
CommonX → Xa → prothrombin (II) → thrombin (IIa) → fibrinBoth

Thrombin is the central amplifier of coagulation. The vitamin K-dependent factors are II, VII, IX and X (plus proteins C and S).

Remember which test goes with which pathway by the letters: PT — "Play Tennis externally" (extrinsic, VII); APTT — the longer name for the longer pathway (intrinsic: XII, XI, IX, VIII). Platelet problems show up in the platelet count and bleeding time, not PT or APTT.

The tooth socket (midterm Ch 5) is this sequence in action: clot formation and platelet retraction in the first hours, fibrin cross-linking over 24 hours, fibrinolysis from day 2 — which is why dry socket risk peaks then.

Thrombocytopenia

Thrombocytopenia is a platelet count below 150 × 10⁹/L; below 20 × 10⁹/L causes spontaneous bleeding and risk of life-threatening haemorrhage. There are three mechanisms:

MechanismCausesNotes
1. Decreased productionMegaloblastic anaemia (B12/folate); marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, metastases, fibrosis); aplastic anaemia (autoimmune, hepatitis-associated, drugs such as chloramphenicol, radiation); toxins and drugs — chemotherapy is the most common cause in practice; alcoholUsually part of pancytopenia: fatigue (anaemia), infection and oral ulcers (neutropenia), bleeding
2. Increased destructionImmune: ITP — autoantibodies to platelet GPIIb/IIIa or GPIb, opsonised platelets destroyed in the spleen (acute in children after a viral infection; chronic in adults, more in women); drug-induced (heparin — HIT type II; quinine; sulfonamides; antiepileptics); neonatal alloimmune. Non-immune: DIC (platelets consumed), TTP (microthrombi shear platelets — medical emergency)Sudden bruising, epistaxis, heavy menses; fever and neurological signs in TTP
3. Increased sequestrationHypersplenism — portal hypertension, cirrhosis, splenomegaly of any causeAn enlarged spleen traps a large share of circulating platelets (the lecture gives 50–90% and 80–90%) despite normal production; usually mild–moderate

Oral signs: petechiae on the buccal mucosa and palate, ecchymoses and purpura, blood blisters, mucosal oozing, bleeding after brushing or minor trauma, and prolonged post-extraction bleeding in undiagnosed cases.

Dental red flags: gingival bleeding out of proportion to periodontal status; recurrent spontaneous oral bleeding; petechiae in a patient not on anticoagulants — request a full blood count. Invasive procedures are avoided below 50 × 10⁹/L (platelet transfusion may be needed).

ITP is the midterm's type II hypersensitivity (Ch 6): antibody against a cell-bound antigen leading to opsonisation and splenic destruction.

Inherited bleeding disorders

von Willebrand disease

The most common inherited bleeding disorder (≈1% of the population), caused by quantitative or qualitative defects in vWF. vWF has two jobs — mediating platelet adhesion via GPIb and carrying and stabilising factor VIII — so vWD impairs primary haemostasis and the bleeding pattern looks like a platelet disorder: easy bruising, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia, prolonged bleeding after extractions.

Labs: normal platelet count but prolonged bleeding time; APTT may be mildly prolonged because factor VIII is low. Treatment: desmopressin (DDAVP), which releases vWF and FVIII from endothelial stores; vWF-containing factor concentrates for severe types.

Haemophilia A and B

Haemophilia AHaemophilia B (Christmas disease)
DeficiencyFactor VIIIFactor IX
Share80–85% of haemophiliaThe remainder
InheritanceX-linked recessive — predominantly males; female carriers may have mild symptoms because of lyonisation (random X-inactivation)
LabsProlonged APTT; normal PT, normal platelet count, normal bleeding time
TreatmentFactor VIII replacement; emicizumab (a FVIII mimetic that bypasses the intrinsic pathway); gene therapy emergingFactor IX replacement; gene therapy emerging
SeverityFactor activityBleeding
Severe<1%Spontaneous bleeding into joints and muscles; haemarthroses → chronic joint destruction; intracranial bleeding risk
Moderate1–5%Bleeding with minor trauma; occasional spontaneous bleeds
Mild5–30%Mainly after surgery, dental extractions or major trauma — may be diagnosed for the first time after an extraction

The bleeding pattern is deep — haemarthroses (knees, ankles, elbows → synovial hypertrophy, cartilage loss, chronic arthropathy) and deep muscle haematomas (an iliopsoas bleed may compress nerves or mimic an acute abdomen) — in contrast to the mucocutaneous pattern of platelet and vWF disorders. Inhibitor antibodies against FVIII develop in 20–30% of severe haemophilia A, making replacement less effective; bypassing agents (e.g. recombinant FVIIa) are then needed.

The two bleeding patterns — the most useful single idea in this section:
Primary haemostasis defect (platelets, vWF) → mucocutaneous: petechiae, gum bleeding, epistaxis, immediate oozing.
Secondary haemostasis defect (clotting factors) → deep: joints, muscles, delayed bleeding after the plug fails.

Other factor deficiencies

Factor XICommon in Ashkenazi Jewish populations; variable bleeding; surgical bleeding more than spontaneous; ↑APTT
Factor XIIProlonged APTT but no bleeding tendency — do not confuse an abnormal test with risk, and do not delay dental care; associated with thrombosis in some studies
Factors VII, V, X, XIIIRare, severe; factor XIII deficiency causes poor wound healing (XIII cross-links fibrin)

Acquired disorders — liver disease and anticoagulants

Liver disease

The liver makes most clotting factors, so liver disease disturbs haemostasis in several ways at once:

  • ↓ synthesis of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X, V, XI) and of fibrinogen (or dysfunctional fibrinogen)
  • ↓ clearance of activated factors → paradoxical thrombosis
  • Thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism (portal hypertension)
  • ↓ vitamin K absorption in cholestasis

Clinically: easy bruising, prolonged PT as the early marker (factor VII has the shortest half-life), both bleeding and thrombosis risk, spider naevi, jaundice, ascites; orally, cheilitis, candidosis and glossitis from malnutrition.

Anticoagulant drugs

DrugTarget / mechanismClinical notes
WarfarinInhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase → depletes factors II, VII, IX, XINR monitoring; many drug and diet interactions (miconazole — Ch 1); stop or adjust only with medical guidance; check INR before invasive procedures
Heparin (UFH / LMWH)Enhances antithrombin → inhibits thrombin and factor XaRapid onset, hospital use; UFH monitored by APTT; LMWH more predictable
DOACsDirect factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban); direct thrombin (IIa) inhibitor (dabigatran)No INR monitoring; shorter half-life; more post-extraction bleeding — timing of the procedure relative to the dose matters

Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel) affect primary haemostasis: normal platelet count, prolonged bleeding time, persistent oozing. Do not stop antiplatelets without medical advice — the thrombotic risk of stopping usually outweighs the bleeding risk, which is managed with local haemostatic measures (sutures, packing, tranexamic acid).

Bleeding disorders — the summary table

DisorderDefectBleeding patternLabsDental note
Thrombocytopenia↓ platelets (production, destruction, sequestration)Mucocutaneous↓ platelets; PT/APTT normalAvoid invasive procedures <50 × 10⁹/L; find the cause
Platelet function (incl. aspirin)Defective adhesion/aggregationGum bleeding, bruisingNormal count; ↑ bleeding timeDon't stop antiplatelets; local haemostasis
von Willebrand disease↓ or faulty vWF; ↓ FVIIIPlatelet-type↑ bleeding time; ± ↑APTT; platelets normalDDAVP (type 1) or concentrate; liaise with haematology
Haemophilia A / B↓ FVIII / ↓ FIX (X-linked)Deep — joints, muscles↑APTT; PT and platelets normalFactor replacement + tranexamic acid, with the haemophilia team
Factor XI deficiency↓ FXISurgical bleeding↑APTTHaematology plan for replacement timing
Factor XII deficiency↓ FXIINone↑APTTNo bleeding risk — don't delay care
Liver disease↓ factor synthesis, ↓ fibrinogen quality, ↓ platelets, ↓ vit KMucocutaneous and deep↑PT early, ↑APTT; ↓ plateletsCheck INR, platelets, fibrinogen; avoid NSAIDs; may need hospital
Vitamin K deficiency↓ γ-carboxylation of II, VII, IX, XSurgical oozing↑PT early, ↑APTT laterReplace vitamin K; find the cause
WarfarinVitamin K antagonistDeep / post-op↑PT / INRCheck INR pre-procedure
Heparin / LMWHPotentiates antithrombinProcedural↑APTT (UFH)Schedule around doses; caution with nerve blocks
DOACsDirect Xa or IIa inhibitionPost-extraction oozingRoutine tests unreliableTiming around the dose

Required reading: Underwood's Pathology, 8th ed., Chapter 13 (Cardiovascular system) and Chapter 23 (Blood and bone marrow — disorders of coagulation and haemostasis); Robbins Basic Pathology.

Drill

Describe the pathogenesis of an atheromatous plaque and explain what makes one likely to rupture.

Endothelial injury (hypertension, smoking, hyperglycaemia, hyperlipidaemia, turbulent flow) increases permeability; LDL enters the intima and is oxidised. Oxidised LDL is chemotactic and pro-inflammatory, inducing VCAM-1 and ICAM-1; monocytes adhere, enter, become macrophages and ingest it, forming foam cells (fatty streak). Cytokines recruit smooth muscle cells from the media, which make collagen and form a fibrous cap over a necrotic lipid core. Rupture is likely with a thin cap, a large lipid core, heavy inflammation (MMPs degrading the cap) and little calcification; rupture exposes thrombogenic contents and causes acute thrombosis.

A patient develops central chest pain while you are giving a local anaesthetic. How do you tell angina from MI, and what is the mechanism behind your test?

Stop, sit the patient up, give GTN. Angina — a fixed stenosis with demand temporarily exceeding supply — settles within minutes with rest and GTN (which dilates coronary arteries and veins, raising supply and lowering preload). Pain lasting more than 20–30 minutes and unrelieved by GTN suggests MI — an occlusive thrombus on a ruptured plaque, which GTN cannot relieve — so call an ambulance and give aspirin if not contraindicated. Confirmation in hospital is raised troponin and ECG changes.

Explain why a patient with left heart failure cannot lie flat in the dental chair.

The failing left ventricle cannot clear blood returning from the lungs, so pulmonary venous pressure is raised. Lying flat increases venous return from the legs, raising pulmonary venous pressure further and pushing fluid into the alveoli — orthopnoea. Treat semi-upright, keep appointments short and monitor oxygen saturation.

Haemophilia A vs von Willebrand disease: compare the defect, bleeding pattern and laboratory findings.

Haemophilia A is X-linked factor VIII deficiency — a secondary haemostasis defect giving deep bleeding into joints and muscles and delayed post-extraction bleeding; APTT prolonged, PT, platelet count and bleeding time normal. vWD (autosomal, ~1%) is deficient or faulty vWF — impaired platelet adhesion, a primary haemostasis defect giving mucocutaneous bleeding (gums, nose, menorrhagia, oozing after extraction); bleeding time prolonged, platelets normal, APTT mildly prolonged because vWF carries FVIII. vWD responds to desmopressin.

A 62-year-old with new pain in the masseters on chewing, a temporal headache and blurred vision in one eye. Diagnosis, mechanism and action?

Giant cell arteritis: granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of the temporal and other cranial arteries, causing ischaemia of the masticatory muscles (jaw claudication) and threatening the ophthalmic artery. Urgent same-day medical referral — untreated it can cause irreversible blindness.

Name the three mechanisms of thrombocytopenia with an example of each, and the oral signs.

Decreased production — chemotherapy, leukaemia or aplastic anaemia (often pancytopenia). Increased destruction — ITP (autoantibodies to GPIIb/IIIa, splenic removal) or DIC/TTP (consumption). Increased sequestration — hypersplenism in cirrhosis with portal hypertension. Oral signs: petechiae, purpura, blood blisters, spontaneous gingival bleeding, prolonged bleeding after extraction.

A patient's pre-operative APTT is prolonged but they have never bled abnormally, even after a previous extraction. What might explain this?

Factor XII deficiency — XII is needed for the APTT test's contact activation but not for haemostasis in the body, so the test is abnormal with no bleeding tendency. It is not a reason to delay dental care. (Lupus anticoagulant is another cause of a prolonged APTT without bleeding.)

6

Chapter 6 · Lecture 9

Respiratory & Musculoskeletal Disorders

Airways, sleep, bone remodelling, osteonecrosis of the jaw and the temporomandibular joint

Two systems with one thing in common: the dentist meets them every day. The respiratory half asks how a patient breathes in the chair and at night; the musculoskeletal half rests on one idea — all bone disease is some form of disordered bone remodelling — and follows it to the jaw, where remodelling is fastest and failure is visible.

Know these cold

  • Central chemoreceptors respond to CO₂/H⁺; carotid bodies to low PaO₂. COPD patients may rely on hypoxic drive — sedatives and high O₂ are hazards
  • Chronic bronchitis: productive cough ≥3 months in 2 consecutive years; smoking first. Asthma: like it, but reversible
  • OSA: pharyngeal collapse despite effort. AHI <5 normal, 5–15 mild, 15–30 moderate, ≥30 severe. CPAP first line; mandibular advancement splint second
  • Osteoclasts resorb (monocyte–macrophage lineage, RANKL); osteoblasts form (mesenchymal); osteocytes sense and coordinate
  • Osteoporosis: less bone, normal mineralisation; resorption exceeds formation
  • MRONJ: exposed bone >8 weeks + anti-resorptive therapy + no jaw radiotherapy; mandible ~65%
  • ORN: necrotic bone in an irradiated field failing to heal for ≥3–6 months; hypovascular, hypoxic, hypocellular; >60 Gy
  • TMD is biopsychosocial; DC/TMD has Axis I (physical) and Axis II (psychosocial)

The respiratory system

RegionStructures and roles
Upper tractNose and nasal cavity (warm, humidify, filter); sinuses (resonance, mucus); pharynx (shared air and food passage); larynx (airway protection, phonation)
Lower tractTrachea (C-shaped cartilage rings, ciliated epithelium); bronchi (cartilage-supported); bronchioles — smooth muscle, no cartilage, the key site of airflow regulation; alveoli (thin-walled gas-exchange sacs; type I and type II pneumocytes)
Conducting zoneNose → terminal bronchioles: conducts, warms, humidifies, filters
Respiratory zoneRespiratory bronchioles → alveoli: gas exchange

Respiratory epithelium

CellFunctionIn disease
Ciliated pseudostratified columnarMain lining of trachea and bronchi; all cells touch the basement membrane; cilia beat upward → mucociliary clearanceSmoking paralyses cilia; squamous metaplasia (midterm Ch 2)
Goblet cellsSecrete mucin to trap particles — with cilia, the mucociliary escalatorGoblet cell hyperplasia in chronic irritation (smoking, chronic bronchitis)
Neuroendocrine cellsRelease peptides and amines (serotonin) affecting airway tone and growthGive rise to carcinoid tumours and small-cell carcinoma
Basal cellsStem cells; regeneration after injuryDrive metaplasia in chronic inflammation
Submucosal glandsMucous and serous secretionHypertrophy contributes to obstruction in chronic bronchitis

Surfactant from type II pneumocytes reduces alveolar surface tension. The lung also has non-respiratory functions: defence against inhaled noxious substances; synthesis, release and metabolism of bradykinin, serotonin and some prostaglandins; and conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II by the lung's endothelial cells (ACE — the link to hypertension, Ch 5).

Control of respiration

ReceptorSiteResponds to
Central chemoreceptorsMedulla↑CO₂ and ↑H⁺ in the CSF — the primary minute-to-minute driver of ventilation
Peripheral chemoreceptorsCarotid bodies (most important) and aortic bodies↓PaO₂ (hypoxaemia); also ↑CO₂ and ↑H⁺ — rapid feedback when oxygen drops

In chronic hypoxia (COPD, chronic lung disease) the carotid bodies become hyperplastic and more sensitive, and patients may rely more on hypoxic drive than on CO₂ drive.

Clinical relevance: sedatives, opioids and benzodiazepines depress the respiratory centres; COPD patients are at risk of CO₂ retention; supplemental oxygen must be used carefully in severe chronic disease, because removing the hypoxic stimulus can reduce ventilation further.

Respiratory disease — classification and symptoms

Respiratory diseases are classified as acute or chronic and by site. Upper tract: infections, sinusitis. Lower tract: acute bronchitis, pneumonia, bronchiolitis, asthma, COPD (chronic bronchitis and emphysema), cystic fibrosis, pulmonary embolism; and granulomatous lung disease (tuberculosis, sarcoidosis).

Symptom / signPathological basis
CoughThe commonest symptom; dry, productive or paroxysmal. Viral infection, asthma, chronic bronchitis, pneumonia, reflux, lung cancer. Persistent cough >3 weeks warrants investigation
Purulent sputumThick yellow-green, neutrophil-rich exudate → bacterial infection (bronchitis, pneumonia, bronchiectasis)
HaemoptysisMucosal ulceration (infection, bronchiectasis), tumour eroding a vessel, pulmonary infarction (PE). Always significant — urgent evaluation
WheezeHigh-pitched expiratory sound from airway narrowing — bronchospasm (asthma), mucus plugging (bronchitis), airway collapse (COPD)
DyspnoeaAirway obstruction, parenchymal disease (pneumonia, fibrosis), pulmonary oedema, pulmonary vascular disease (PE), cardiac disease
CyanosisIncreased deoxygenated haemoglobin; central vs peripheral; seen at lips, tongue, nail beds
ClubbingBulbous enlargement of the fingertips in chronic hypoxia — lung cancer, bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease, cystic fibrosis
Chest painPleuritic (sharp, worse on inspiration) → pneumonia, pleuritis, PE; pressure-like → cardiac; reproducible on palpation → musculoskeletal

Aetiological factors

FactorExamples
GeneticCystic fibrosis — defective CFTR → thick mucus, recurrent infection, bronchiectasis. α1-antitrypsin deficiency → unopposed neutrophil elastase → early-onset emphysema
InfectionViral (influenza, RSV, rhinovirus); bacterial (pneumococcus, staphylococcus, H. influenzae) → pneumonia, abscess; TB → granulomas with cavitation
SmokingLung cancer, chronic bronchitis, emphysema; impaired mucociliary clearance + chronic inflammation
Air pollutionParticulates, nitrogen oxides, ozone → asthma exacerbations, chronic inflammation, infection
OccupationalPneumoconiosis (coal, silica) → fibrosis and restrictive disease; asbestosis → interstitial fibrosis, mesothelioma and lung cancer risk

Burden: chronic respiratory conditions affect about 30% of Australians (allergic rhinitis, asthma, chronic sinusitis, COPD, and others such as bronchiectasis and OSA), with higher rates in older people, smokers, people with occupational or pollution exposure, Indigenous Australians and those with poor nutrition. Respiratory disease is about 8% of the total disease burden — the sixth leading cause, behind cancer, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, mental and substance-use disorders, and injuries — and OSA is probably underdiagnosed.

Sinusitis

Sinusitis is inflammation of the epithelial lining of the paranasal sinuses, causing mucosal oedema and increased secretions. The main organisms are streptococci (including pneumococci), staphylococci and Haemophilus influenzae. Pain may be unilateral or bilateral; the sinus is often tender and swollen to palpation; sore throat is common. It is often confused with migraine — and with dental pain.

Why it mimics toothache, and how to tell

The roots of the maxillary posterior teeth and the superior alveolar nerves lie against the floor of the maxillary antrum, so sinus inflammation is felt in the teeth. Conversely, roughly 25% of maxillary sinusitis is associated with dental infection or dental causes (a periapical infection or an oro-antral communication).

TestPoints to sinusitis
Head movementPain worse on bending forward or moving the head
Vitality testingTeeth vital
Palpation / percussionSeveral adjacent upper teeth tender to percussion, not one; tenderness over the sinus
Radiographs / CBCT or MDCTMucosal thickening or fluid level in the antrum; no periapical pathology

Also consider migraine and parafunction/myalgia. Chronic sinus disease causes chronic mouth breathing, raising the risk of OSA, gingivitis, halitosis and dry mouth; decongestants also dry the mouth.

COPD

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a chronic disease of difficulty in expiration, comprising chronic bronchitis and emphysema, both characterised by chronic airflow obstruction during normal breathing.

Chronic bronchitis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the bronchial epithelium defined clinically by a productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, with reduced forced expiration, wheeze and breathlessness, and a historical male predominance. Cigarette smoking is the major cause; environmental pollution and dust are second.

Pathogenesis

  1. Impaired mucociliary clearanceCilia damaged; mucus stagnates.
  2. HypersecretionIrritation → goblet cell hyperplasia and submucosal gland hypertrophy → thick mucus.
  3. Airway wall thickeningOedema and fibrosis → irreversible narrowing of the airways; damaged fibroelastic tissue (emphysema: alveolar walls destroyed, airways collapse on expiration).
  4. ConsequencesDiminished gas exchange → hypoxaemia → pulmonary hypertension → right heart failure (cor pulmonale, Ch 5) and respiratory failure.

Oral manifestations and dental management

Orally: smoking-related lesions — smoker's melanosis, nicotinic stomatitis, dysplasia. Management:

  • Preserve the patient's respiratory capacity — treat in a more upright position
  • Avoid CNS-depressant drugs (sedatives, opioids)
  • Oxygen may be needed (with care in CO₂ retainers)
  • Consider supplemental corticosteroids in patients on long-term steroids

Asthma

Asthma is an intermittent respiratory disorder of airway hyper-reactivity to various stimuli, producing recurrent bronchial smooth-muscle spasm, inflammation and swelling of the bronchial mucosa, and hypersecretion of viscid mucus with sputum plugging. Prevalence in Australia is about 11%; all ages, more common in childhood. Airway narrowing raises resistance, especially on expiration; lung distal to mucus plugs becomes hyperinflated.

Risk factorsTypes
Family history; atopy (allergies, hay fever)Extrinsic (allergic, atopic — type I hypersensitivity, midterm Ch 6); intrinsic (non-allergic); exercise-induced; drug-induced (aspirin); infectious

The pathogenesis is not dissimilar to chronic bronchitis — wall thickening, mucous hypersecretion, gas trapping — but asthma has a reversible component. An attack brings wheezing, coughing, cyanosis, sweating, tachycardia and chest tightness.

Inhaled medications

ClassExampleAction and use
β2-adrenergic agonist (bronchodilator)Salbutamol (Ventolin)Delivered directly to the airway. Relaxes airway smooth muscle; reduces fluid leakage and mast-cell cytokine release. The reliever for acute symptoms, complementary in long-term management
Inhaled corticosteroid (± long-acting β2 agonist)Symbicort (budesonide + formoterol)Long-term control (prevention); inhaled route minimises systemic effects. Use a spacer and rinse the mouth afterwards — to prevent oral candidosis (Ch 1)
Dental: ask patients to bring their inhaler to every appointment; reduce anxiety; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs in aspirin-sensitive asthma; look for candidosis and median rhomboid glossitis in steroid-inhaler users.

Obstructive sleep apnoea

OSA is a sleep disorder of recurrent narrowing or collapse of the pharyngeal airway during sleep despite ongoing breathing effort, causing acute disturbances of blood gases and fragmented sleep.

Types and scoring

TypeMechanism
Central (5–10%)Decreased ventilatory drive — no effort
ObstructiveAirway collapse despite effort
Complex / mixedBoth
EventScoring
ApnoeaAirflow drop ≥90% of baseline for ≥10 seconds
HypopnoeaDrop ≥30% for ≥10 seconds with ≥3% oxygen desaturation or an arousal
RERA(Optional) ~10 s of increased effort ending in arousal without meeting apnoea or hypopnoea criteria
SeverityApnoea–hypopnoea index (events per hour)
Normal<5
Mild5 to <15
Moderate15 to <30
Severe≥30

Consequences, screening and risk factors

Low oxygen plus broken sleep produce excessive daytime sleepiness, snoring, morning headaches, poor memory and irritability, depression, reduced libido, and are associated with cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, diabetes, obesity, GERD, bruxism and cancer. About 1 in 5 adults has mild OSA and 1 in 15 moderate-to-severe; 80% remain undiagnosed. Snoring is a symptom to take seriously.

Screening: examination and questionnaires — STOP-BANG, Epworth Sleepiness Scale. Diagnosis: polysomnography (PSG) or home/portable studies. Risk factors: male sex, obesity, hypertension, upper-airway or facial abnormalities, smoking, family history, large neck circumference.

What a dentist sees

Structural: narrow palate, retrognathia, deviated septum, thick soft palate, large uvula, large tonsils, a high Mallampati score. Signs: parafunction, scalloped tongue, oral dryness at night.

Treatment

CPAPOral appliance (mandibular advancement splint)
PlaceGold standard, first-lineSecond-line
MechanismA pneumatic splint preventing nocturnal collapse of the upper airwayAdvances the mandible: stabilises the airway against collapse, widens the lateral airway (especially the velopharynx behind the soft palate), displaces the tongue forward
BenefitQuality of life, sleepiness, neuropsychological performance, hypertension; mean AHI reduction 25, Epworth reduction 2.23Many designs; complete response (AHI <5) ~37% overall, higher in mild OSA
DrawbackPoor complianceBetter compliance; side effects (below)

Other options: upper airway surgery, hypoglossal nerve stimulators, weight loss. MAS side effects: jaw and TMJ discomfort, changes in tooth alignment or bite, excess salivation or dry mouth, tooth and gum soreness, throat irritation, tension headaches, jaw-muscle fatigue, initial difficulty speaking or swallowing, and occasionally worse snoring or apnoea.

Bone biology

Bone is a dynamic, metabolically active tissue. Millions of remodelling units are active at once, replacing old or damaged bone, to maintain strength, repair microdamage from daily loading, regulate mineral homeostasis, and adapt to new demands (occlusal forces, orthodontic movement). Its integrity depends on coupling: resorption by osteoclasts exactly matched by formation by osteoblasts. In disease, coupling is lost:

FailureExample
Resorption exceeds formationOsteoporosis
Formation defective or disorganisedOsteomalacia (poor mineralisation), Paget disease
Remodelling spatially or temporally abnormalFibrous dysplasia, tumour infiltration

Key unifying concept: all bone disease represents some form of disordered bone remodelling — whether metabolic, inflammatory, infective, neoplastic or genetic.

Functions of bone

  1. Structural support and load bearingPosture, locomotion, mastication; failure → deformity and fracture.
  2. ProtectionBrain, spinal cord, thoracic organs.
  3. Mineral homeostasisThe main reservoir of calcium, phosphate and magnesium, under PTH, vitamin D and calcitonin; disruption → hypo- or hypercalcaemia.
  4. HaemopoiesisMarrow diseases (myeloma, metastases, fibrosis) present with anaemia, infection or bleeding.

Why the jaws are special: a high remodelling rate, constant mechanical loading, and rapid response to systemic metabolic change — so the jaws are early indicators of metabolic bone disease and especially vulnerable to impaired healing.

Cortical vs trabecular bone

Cortical (compact)Trabecular (cancellous)
StructureDense outer shell; Haversian systemsLattice of thin plates and struts; very high surface area; richly vascular
TurnoverRelatively inactiveMetabolically active, remodels rapidly
WhereShafts of long bones; outer shell everywhereVertebral bodies, pelvis, proximal femur, maxilla and mandible
In diseaseAffected later; critical for overall strengthAffected early in osteoporosis; common site for metastases; sensitive to endocrine change

The predominance of trabecular bone in the jaws explains early radiographic changes in systemic bone disease, fragility in osteoporosis, altered implant stability and healing, and susceptibility to osteonecrosis and pathological fracture.

The three bone cells

CellOriginFunction
OsteoclastMonocyte–macrophage lineage (the bone–immune link)Large multinucleated resorbing cell. Seals onto bone forming a resorption lacuna; secretes H⁺ via proton pumps (dissolves mineral) and cathepsins (digest type I collagen). Regulated by PTH, vitamin D and the RANK–RANKL–OPG system
OsteoblastMesenchymal stem cells (shared with fibroblasts, chondrocytes, adipocytes)Synthesises osteoid (unmineralised matrix rich in type I collagen); alkaline phosphatase promotes mineralisation; controls osteoclasts by expressing RANKL (stimulates) and osteoprotegerin (decoy that blocks RANKL). Becomes osteocyte or lining cell
OsteocyteOsteoblast trapped in its own matrixThe central regulator of remodelling: a network linked by canaliculi; mechanosensor detecting strain and microdamage; signals osteoblasts and osteoclasts
RANK–RANKL–OPG in one line: osteoblasts make RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and switches them on; they also make OPG, a decoy receptor that mops RANKL up. The RANKL:OPG ratio sets the rate of resorption — and denosumab is simply an artificial OPG.

The remodelling cycle

  1. ActivationMicrodamage, mechanical stress or hormones recruit osteoclast precursors to a site.
  2. ResorptionOsteoclasts resorb a discrete area over several weeks, releasing calcium and phosphate.
  3. ReversalOsteoclasts undergo apoptosis; mononuclear cells prepare the surface.
  4. FormationOsteoblasts lay down osteoid.
  5. MineralisationCalcium and phosphate are deposited into the osteoid.

Remodelling is asynchronous: about one million sites are active at once, and the adult skeleton is effectively renewed about every 7 years (lecture figure). Uncoupling of resorption and formation is the fundamental mechanism of metabolic bone disease.

Bone pain, fracture and osteoporosis

Why bone hurts

The mineralised matrix itself is not innervated; pain comes from associated structures:

Periosteal stretchingThe periosteum is richly innervated; expansion from tumour, infection or callus gives severe, well-localised pain
Raised intraosseous pressureInflammation, marrow infiltration or haemorrhage inside a rigid compartment
Inflammatory mediatorsCytokines and prostaglandins sensitise nociceptors
MicrofracturesIn weakened bone, microdamage accumulates faster than it is repaired → chronic pain

Other bone signs and their basis: fracture after trivial injury (weakened bone); deformity (abnormal growth or remodelling, malunion); hypercalcaemia (extensive tumour erosion, PTH from a parathyroid adenoma, or PTHrP from visceral tumours such as bronchogenic carcinoma).

Fractures

A fracture occurs when load exceeds strength. A fracture after minimal or trivial injury indicates underlying bone disease — a pathological fracture — in osteoporosis, osteomalacia, tumour infiltration or Paget disease.

Fracture healing needs adequate blood supply, immobilisation and stability, and viable bone ends (the callus sequence of the midterm Ch 5). It is delayed by excessive movement, infection, corticosteroids, poor nutrition and ischaemia. The same principles govern socket healing, jaw fractures and implant osseointegration.

Osteoporosis

DefinitionA metabolic bone disease of reduced bone mass with normal mineralisation of the remaining bone, increasing the risk of fragility fractures
PathogenesisUncoupled remodelling — resorption exceeds formation → progressive net bone loss
EpidemiologyElderly; marked female predominance; accelerated loss after menopause (oestrogen restrains osteoclasts); trabecular bone first
ClinicalAsymptomatic until fracture: vertebral compression (loss of height, kyphosis), hip and wrist fractures
Osteoporosis vs osteomalacia — the classic contrast: osteoporosis = less bone, normally mineralised; osteomalacia = normal amount of matrix, poorly mineralised (vitamin D deficiency).

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ)

MRONJ is an adverse effect of anti-resorptive medications, used for osteoporosis and in oncology to prevent skeletal complications of metastases — most commonly bisphosphonates (pamidronate, zoledronate) and denosumab, less commonly anti-angiogenic agents.

Diagnostic criteria

  1. Exposed boneIn the maxillofacial region (or bone that can be probed through a fistula), persisting more than 8 weeks
  2. Drug historyCurrent or previous anti-resorptive therapy
  3. No jaw radiotherapyNo history of radiation therapy to the jaws — which would make it ORN instead (and no metastatic disease of the jaw)

How the drugs work, and why the jaw fails

BisphosphonatesDenosumab
Bind strongly to bone mineral, are taken up by osteoclasts during resorption, and disrupt osteoclast metabolism → osteoclast apoptosis → reduced turnover. Because they stay bound in bone, their effect persists for years. May have anti-angiogenic effectsA monoclonal antibody against RANKL → prevents activation of osteoclast precursors → reduced osteoclast formation, function and survival → marked suppression of resorption. Does not bind bone, so the effect wears off months after the last dose; no proven anti-angiogenic effect (normal vascularity histologically)

Key concept: suppressed bone turnover limits the jaw's ability to repair microdamage, predisposing to non-healing exposed bone, particularly after dental trauma. The jaw is hit because it remodels fastest, is thinly covered by mucosa that is easily breached, and is constantly exposed to the oral microbiome.

Epidemiology and risk factors

WhoMean age ≈70; strong female predominance
DoseLow-dose anti-resorptives (osteoporosis) → very low incidence; high-dose IV therapy (oncology) → substantially higher risk; risk rises with duration (cumulative exposure, no clear threshold)
Local triggersInvasive dental procedures, especially extractions; periodontal disease and pre-existing infection; mandibular extractions riskier than maxillary
ModifiersCorticosteroids, chemotherapy, diabetes, renal disease, poor oral hygiene, anti-angiogenic drugs

Aetiopathogenesis is multifactorial and uncertain: suppressed bone turnover + local infection and biofilm + impaired healing. Dental disease often acts as the initiating event, and infection is considered a key trigger.

Presentation and management

Usually exposed bone; non-exposed variants (pain, a fistula probing to bone) are recognised. Distribution: mandible ≈65%, maxilla ≈28%, both ≈6%. May be painless, or present with pain, infection, soft-tissue inflammation and, in advanced cases, pathological fracture.

Management is stage-dependent and primarily conservative, aiming to prevent progression, control pain and manage infection: eliminate dental infection; excellent oral hygiene; chlorhexidine mouth rinses; systemic antibiotics only for clinical infection; remove mobile sequestra. Surgery (debridement or resection to bleeding vital bone, with primary closure) is reserved for advanced or refractory cases.

Prevention is the dentist's job: ideally, make the mouth healthy before anti-resorptive therapy starts, and prefer endodontics over extraction where possible in patients already on high-dose therapy.

Osteoradionecrosis (ORN)

ORN is exposed necrotic bone in a previously irradiated field that fails to heal for ≥3–6 months, in the absence of recurrent tumour.

SiteMost commonly the posterior mandible
IncidenceAbout 4–5% with modern IMRT (higher rates are reported); IMRT/VMAT reduce but do not eliminate risk compared with older 3D-CRT
TimingHighest risk 4 months to 2 years after radiotherapy — but can present many years later
Risk factorsHigher dose, especially >60 Gy; tumours of base of tongue, tonsil, hypopharynx; smoking and alcohol; poor oral hygiene; dental extractions before or after RT; mandibular tumour invasion or surgery

Pathogenesis — radiation-induced fibroatrophy

  1. Endothelial damage and inflammationSmall vessels are injured and obliterated.
  2. Abnormal fibroblast activity → fibrosis
  3. Loss of osteoblastsReduced capacity to regenerate bone.
  4. ResultBone becomes hypovascular, hypoxic and hypocellular — fragile and prone to necrosis after minor trauma or infection.

Presentation: usually exposed bone (a subset has intact mucosa with radiographic bone loss); pain, dysaesthesia, halitosis, dysgeusia, food impaction; may progress to infection, fistula or pathological fracture.

Prevention and treatment

PreventionTreatment
Comprehensive dental assessment before radiotherapy; ideally complete extractions ≥1 month before RT (reduces but does not eliminate risk); post-RT extractions carry significantly higher risk; optimise hygiene; stop smoking and alcohol; antibiotic prophylaxis may be considered (limited evidence); lifelong dental follow-upAim: symptom control and preventing progression. Conservative first: chlorhexidine rinses, removal of loose sequestra, antibiotics for secondary infection. Hyperbaric oxygen shows limited benefit. Emerging: pentoxifylline + tocopherol ± clodronate (PENTOCLO). Surgery for advanced/refractory disease: sequestrectomy early; segmental resection and reconstruction when advanced

MRONJ vs ORN

MRONJORN
CauseAnti-resorptive (± anti-angiogenic) drugsRadiotherapy to the jaws
Core defectSuppressed bone turnover — bone cannot repair microdamageHypovascular, hypoxic, hypocellular bone — fibroatrophy
Time criterionExposed >8 weeksFails to heal ≥3–6 months
ExclusionNo jaw radiotherapyNo recurrent tumour
Usual siteMandible (~65%)Posterior mandible
Commonest triggerExtractionExtraction (especially after RT)

The temporomandibular joint and TMD

Musculoskeletal conditions are a heterogeneous group affecting bone, cartilage, muscle, nerve and vessel, with multisystem overlap and coexisting metabolic and ageing disease. They are very common — about 50% of adults report chronic musculoskeletal pain — and cause great morbidity but little mortality. Their signs map onto pathology: joint pain (inflammation or abnormal load stimulating capsule and synovial nerve endings), deformity (synovial swelling, effusion, erosion, abnormal subchondral remodelling, malalignment), restricted movement (swelling, fibrosis, pain), and systemic features in immune-mediated arthritis.

Temporomandibular disorder (TMD) is pain and dysfunction of the TMJs and/or the masticatory muscles. Prevalence 5–12% (US), with 15% of these becoming chronic; incidence about 4% per year, half still symptomatic 6 months later (OPPERA study); highest prevalence at 18–45 years.

Aetiology — from single causes to the biopsychosocial model

Historically one-dimensional theories blamed the joint, the muscles, or occlusion. There is good evidence that occlusal variables alone are not aetiological factors in TMD, and physical factors alone are insufficient to explain its onset and presentation. TMD is now understood through Engel's (1977) biopsychosocial model — biological, psychological and social factors interacting.

Risk factor groupDetail
PhysicalFemale sex (only slightly); macrotrauma — prolonged wide opening (long dental appointment, GA); clenching/bruxism; trauma in a susceptible individual; self-reported joint noises; parafunctional habits; genetics
PsychologicalHigh depression, anxiety and perceived stress; somatisation in up to ~77% and depression in up to ~60% of TMD patients; frequency of somatic symptoms was the strongest psychosocial predictor of TMD onset in OPPERA; somatic awareness predicts progression from acute to chronic
Other body painWidespread pain, chronic headache/migraine, IBS, low back pain, pelvic pain; the most severe TMD carries the greatest comorbid pain burden
General healthPoorer health → more TMD: respiratory and neural conditions, 3+ medications, smoking, poor sleep

Bruxism and sleep

Bruxism is awake (AB) or sleep (SB), with biological, psychological and exogenous causes. In a Dutch population study, AB affected about 5% of adults and SB about 16.5%. Its role in TMD is controversial, but many accept it as a risk factor; the proposed pathway is stress sensitivity and anxious traits → bruxism → TMD pain, modulated by psychosocial factors.

About 35% of people report frequent poor sleep. Sleep and pain are bidirectional, but the effect of poor sleep on pain is greater than the effect of pain on sleep; poor sleep predicts first-onset TMD (partly mediated by stress). Screening sleep is recommended — the PSQI with a cut-off of 5/21.

Diagnosis — DC/TMD

The biopsychosocial model was built into the RDC/TMD (Dworkin and LeResche, 1992), validated as the DC/TMD (2014): validated criteria for research and clinical use, non-hierarchical (multiple diagnoses allowed), with a dual-axis framework — Axis I: physical diagnoses of the common muscle and joint disorders; Axis II: psychosocial and behavioural screening questionnaires.

Axis I groupDiagnoses
Pain-related TMDMyalgia (local myalgia, myofascial pain, myofascial pain with referral); arthralgia; headache attributed to TMD
Intra-articular TMDDisc displacement with reduction; with reduction and intermittent locking; without reduction with limited opening; without reduction without limited opening; degenerative joint disease; subluxation

Intra-articular disorders — disc displacement

An intracapsular biomechanical disorder of the condyle–disc complex: in the closed-mouth position the disc lies anterior to the condylar head. Displacement is most commonly anterior, then antero-lateral. Asymptomatic displacements are common — about a third of volunteers on TMJ MRI. Definitive diagnosis requires imaging (MRI).

TypeWhat happensClinical
With reductionThe disc is anterior at rest but reduces (returns onto the condyle) on openingOpening click (often a reciprocal click on closing); normal range
With reduction and intermittent lockingSometimes fails to reduceBrief catching or locking episodes
Without reduction, with limited openingThe disc stays in front and blocks condylar translation"Closed lock" — limited opening, deviation to the affected side, no click
Without reduction, without limited openingChronic non-reducing disc; tissues have adaptedOpening has recovered

Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis of the TMJ

OsteoarthritisRheumatoid arthritis
NatureNon-inflammatory, focal degenerative disorder of synovial joints, of articular cartilage and subchondral bone; the most common joint disease; rises with age; weight-bearing jointsChronic multisystem inflammatory (autoimmune) disorder of the synovial membrane — oedema, cell accumulation, synovial proliferation
PathogenesisRetrodiscal degeneration, disc displacement or perforation → condyle articulates directly → cartilage loss, bone flattening/erosion; abnormal loadingBreakdown of self-tolerance; mixed type III and IV hypersensitivity; synoviocyte proliferation → oedematous hyperplastic pannus eroding cartilage and bone
Imaging / tissuesBone: marginal osteophytes, subarticular cysts, subchondral sclerosis. Soft tissue: mild reactive synovitis, capsular swelling. Joint: asymmetric space loss, subluxation, malalignmentErosions; secondary osteoarthritis
ClinicalCrepitus; opening restricted or normal; joint or muscle pain or none; occasional inflammatory signs; more common in womenPain in active disease; restricted opening; morning stiffness (especially neck); swelling uncommon at the TMJ; "my bite doesn't fit" — condylar resorption shortens the ramus, typically causing an anterior open bite; crepitus from secondary OA
Connects to the midterm: RA is autoimmunity (Ch 7) using hypersensitivity types III and IV (Ch 6), and the pannus is chronic inflammation (Ch 4) destroying a joint.

Summary

  • Respiratory and musculoskeletal disease are highly prevalent and drive chronic morbidity.
  • COPD, asthma, sinusitis and OSA bear directly on dental assessment, treatment planning and safety.
  • Bone health depends on coupled remodelling; its disruption underlies osteoporosis, pathological fracture, MRONJ and ORN.
  • The jaws are especially vulnerable — high turnover, trabecular architecture, constant mechanical and microbial challenge.
  • The dentist's role: risk identification, prevention, early recognition and multidisciplinary care.

Required reading: Underwood's Pathology, 8th ed., Chapters 14 and 25; Robbins Basic Pathology.

Drill

A patient with severe COPD is anxious about an extraction. What three things about their physiology change how you manage them?

They have chronic airflow obstruction and impaired gas exchange, so they desaturate easily — treat semi-upright and keep sessions short. Their ventilation may rely on hypoxic drive, so CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids) and high-flow oxygen can reduce breathing and cause CO₂ retention — avoid sedation and use oxygen carefully. If on long-term corticosteroids, consider steroid cover; and look for smoking-related mucosal lesions.

Asthma vs chronic bronchitis: what is shared and what is different?

Both narrow the airways through wall thickening, mucous hypersecretion and gas trapping. Chronic bronchitis is defined by productive cough for 3 months in 2 consecutive years, is caused mainly by smoking, and its narrowing is irreversible. Asthma is intermittent airway hyper-reactivity — often atopic (type I hypersensitivity) — with bronchospasm that is reversible with bronchodilators such as salbutamol.

Explain how a mandibular advancement splint treats OSA and why it is second-line.

Advancing the mandible pulls the tongue and soft tissues forward, stabilising the pharynx against collapse and widening the lateral airway, especially behind the soft palate. CPAP — a pneumatic splint holding the airway open — is more effective and remains first-line; the splint is second-line but better tolerated, with complete response in about a third of patients overall (more in mild OSA), and side effects including TMJ discomfort and occlusal change.

A 74-year-old woman on IV zoledronate for bone metastases has exposed bone in the lower molar socket 10 weeks after extraction. Name the condition, give the criteria, and explain the mechanism.

MRONJ. Criteria: exposed bone in the maxillofacial region for more than 8 weeks; current or previous anti-resorptive therapy; no radiotherapy to the jaws. Zoledronate binds bone mineral and is taken up by resorbing osteoclasts, causing their apoptosis; turnover is suppressed so the jaw cannot repair microdamage or remodel the socket, and infection from the oral biofilm (a key trigger) establishes in the non-healing bone. Risk is high because the dose is oncological and IV. Management is conservative: chlorhexidine, antibiotics only if infected, removal of loose sequestra.

Why is a post-radiotherapy extraction in the posterior mandible high-risk, and what should have happened beforehand?

Radiation (especially >60 Gy) damages endothelium and osteoblasts and causes fibrosis, leaving bone hypovascular, hypoxic and hypocellular — unable to heal the wound, so osteoradionecrosis follows. A comprehensive dental assessment before RT, with any doubtful teeth extracted ideally at least a month before treatment, and lifelong follow-up with excellent hygiene.

A patient clicks on opening; one morning the click stops and they can open only 25 mm, deviating to the left. What has happened?

Disc displacement with reduction (the click is the disc reducing onto the condyle) has progressed to disc displacement without reduction with limited opening — a "closed lock" of the left TMJ: the anteriorly displaced disc no longer reduces and blocks translation of the left condyle, so the jaw deviates toward the affected side. MRI confirms.

A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis says "my bite doesn't fit any more". Explain.

RA is an autoimmune synovitis (mixed type III and IV hypersensitivity) in which proliferating synovium forms a pannus that erodes cartilage and bone. Bilateral resorption of the condyles shortens the rami; the mandible rotates down and back, the molars contact first and an anterior open bite develops.

Things a dentist finds firstCh 1 HIV and HCV oral lesions; Ch 4 early oral cancer; Ch 5 petechiae and gingival bleeding in thrombocytopenia, vWD or haemophilia after extraction; GCA jaw claudication; Ch 6 OSA (retrognathia, scalloped tongue, bruxism); MRONJ and ORN.
